about: the second reader's comparison of named theorems of the background with their published statements (verdict, comparison, sources with places)

Attached.isLabelledAt.verdict: The books and papers give parameter compatibility; the compact squarefree-label predicate needs a separate identification
Attached.isLabelledAt.comparison: Take an eigenform f on the standard definite unitary group of nonzero rank over a CM field with Weil data, a split place w, A over w and an attached r. The product-label hypothesis explicitly requires a monic squarefree nonzero-constant term label c of degree d, separability of c∏(X−xχ) before multiplicities, d+Σt_i=|n|, and a local representation-label condition. The conclusion gives local finite type (finite inertia away from ℓ or potentially crystalline above ℓ), the weight jumps at embeddings above ℓ, and the labelled predicate for c∏(X−xχ)^t. This predicate tests only inertia elements s with the specified tame exponent a of level d!, and forms Q by transforming the roots using ι(T^a). Away from ℓ it requires Q(r(s))=0 and det r(s)=∏roots Q. Above ℓ it uses linear period Frobenius for the Weil pair. Taylor–Yoshida concerns v∤ℓ. BLGGT II, Theorem 1.1 at v|ℓ, gives equal semisimplifications with a monodromy bound, strengthened to Frobenius-semisimplified equality under Shin-regularity. The comparison papers start with eligible GL automorphic representations. Identifying the project's finite Green label and torus characters with the normalized local parameter and passing through its restricted definition of attachment and its period ring requires further results. The compact source uses cyclic base change and the eigencharacter comparison. A statement for arbitrary Frobenius here would exceed the literal labelled predicate.
sources: T. Barnet-Lamb, T. Gee, D. Geraghty and R. Taylor, Local-global compatibility for ℓ=p, II, Ann. Sci. ENS 47 (2014), §1, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2, p. 170. The ordering gives equal semisimplifications and bounds monodromy. Full Frobenius-semisimplified equality is stated at Shin-regular weight.

R. Taylor and T. Yoshida, Compatibility of local and global Langlands correspondences, Theorem A, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 20 (2007), pp. 467–468, author preprint p. 1. The local representation is Frobenius-semisimplified and carries the paper's dual and |det| twist.
Pinned definition of HasProductLabel, including separability and the block ranks.
IsTameExponent requires s in inertia and IsLabelledAt quantifies through this predicate.
Pinned definitions of good type, finite type, jumps and PolyKillsAt in the two residue-characteristic cases.

AutChar.HasWeight.L_ne_zero.verdict: Real-axis specialization of Hecke nonvanishing for a nonzero angular weight vector, with a finite Euler-factor adjustment.
AutChar.HasWeight.L_ne_zero.comparison: For a CM field E with a CM type, ν an automorphic character of the norm-one torus with weight vector e and tame part ψ, e≠0 means at least one component is nonzero. For a finite set S of finite primes and real s≥1 the project asserts ν.L S s≠0. Its unitary Hecke character is χ(x)=ν(x/x̄); the angular type of χ is 2e, so χ² is nontrivial. The primitive finite L-function is nonzero on Re(s)=1 by Ramakrishnan and Valenza, Theorem 7-28, and for Re(s)>1 by the absolutely convergent Euler product. The project defines a function of real s by extension from s>1. It suppresses S∪S̄ and takes χ at a chosen uniformizer at every other prime, even a ramified prime. The latter differs from the conventional primitive ramified factor 1. There are finitely many such primes, and each added or removed factor is invertible near each real s≥1 since |χ(π)|=1 and Nπ>1. This also identifies the right-limit value at 1. The stated boundary and the nonquadratic case are narrower than the published nonvanishing theorem. Tate's cited Main Theorem 4.4.1 gives meromorphic continuation and the functional equation; the boundary nonvanishing requires a further argument.
sources: D. Ramakrishnan and R. J. Valenza, Fourier Analysis on Number Fields (1999), §7.7, Theorem 7-28, p. 289 and (7.16), proof pp. 289–292, including the nonquadratic case. This gives the precise nonvanishing theorem and reduction to the finite L-function.
J. Tate, Fourier analysis in number fields and Hecke's zeta-functions, Cassels–Fröhlich, ch. XV, §4.4, Main Theorem 4.4.1, p. 339, for the global zeta-integral continuation and exceptional poles.
Pinned heckeCoeff and real extension, EulerProduct.lean 113–124. Eventual unramifiedness is in the same file at line 99.
Pinned definition of the partial product and doubled infinity type, AutCharLFunction.lean 49–69.

AutChar.exists_hasWeight_of_prod_eq_one.verdict: The cited full idèle-class character existence result has a different domain and compatibility condition
AutChar.exists_hasWeight_of_prod_eq_one.comparison: A CM type on E fixes a complex lift Φ_v at each infinite place. Give integer exponents e(v), a finite set S of finite places, and multiplicative characters ψ_w of the residue fields, trivial outside S. Assume the product of the Φ_v(u)^e(v) and of ψ_w(u mod w), w in S, is one for every rational norm-one u integral at all finite places. Lean produces a continuous circle-valued character on the norm-one adèles, trivial on rational norm-one elements, with the prescribed character formula on all norm-one adèles whose finite part is integral. Weil's discussion concerns full idèle-class groups. Raghuram §3.1 Proposition 13 gives full multiplicative-group characters with prescribed finite and infinite components under compatibility on all ordinary units. Section 4.3 Proposition 25 allows some modulus for a prescribed pure infinity type and leaves the finite component unspecified. Neither statement in these places gives the norm-one torus assertion with exactly its weaker unit criterion. The Lean proof instead extends a character of the integral norm-one subgroup over the rational points and then uses a finite class quotient and an open subgroup to verify circle values and continuity.
sources: A. Weil, On a certain type of characters of the idèle-class group of an algebraic number-field, Tokyo–Nikko proceedings (1956), pp. 1–7, especially pp. 2–3 on the unit and finite-index extension conditions, equation (3).
A. Raghuram, Notes on the arithmetic of Hecke L-functions, §3.1, equation (12) and Proposition 13, pp. 9–10 of the preprint.
Raghuram, §4.3.2, Proposition 25, p. 17. This existence theorem prescribes the pure infinity type only.
Pinned definitions of AutChar and HasWeight, CharacterDefs.lean, lines 16–60.

BaseLevel.exists_higman_operator.verdict: Classical freeness assumes trivial stabilizers; the declaration constructs a trace equal to a stabilizer multiple
BaseLevel.exists_higman_operator.comparison: Fix ℓ and a complex-to-ℓ-adic identification, a CM type, finite matrix and auxiliary indices, a definite hermitian space and weight, a BaseLevel D and Taylor–Wiles places of modulus ℓ^ν. In D every relevant rational stabilizer order divides the natural number c. For any finite group Δ and any injective homomorphism into the product of residue GL groups, Lean constructs a lattice-preserving endomorphism Ψ with Σ_g ρ(g⁻¹) Ψ ρ(g)=c·id. No assumption makes c invertible, and c may be zero. Taylor–Wiles Theorem 2 and CHT Lemma 3.3.1 establish freeness for particular auxiliary actions, in CHT at sufficiently small level with trivial stabilizers. Higman's criterion uses the identity, applicable after division by c only when allowed. The general case here has weaker output but allows nontrivial stabilizers and arbitrary finite embedded Δ. An orbit-count construction with weights for stabilizer orders is required and occurs in the Lean proof. CHT Lemma 3.1.3 gives a different local representation assertion.
sources: L. Clozel, M. Harris and R. Taylor, Automorphy for some ℓ-adic lifts of automorphic mod ℓ Galois representations, Publ. Math. IHÉS 108 (2008), §3.3, Lemma 3.3.1, p. 99. Lemma 3.1.3, p. 84, concerns unramified GLₙ-representations.

R. Taylor and A. Wiles, Ring-theoretic properties of certain Hecke algebras, Theorem 2 and Proposition 1, author copy pp. 5, 7. The former is freeness of the Hecke algebra over the auxiliary group ring and the latter treats localized cohomology.
M. Broué, Higman criterion revisited, p. 1, classical criterion stated in the abstract. Relative trace equal to the identity characterizes projectivity over a field.
Pinned BaseLevel hypotheses and the divisor c.

Bcris.verdict: The compact definition presents Colmez's B_max.
Bcris.comparison: AmaxStructure.lean:142–151 completes A_inf[X]/(pX−ξ) p-adically, inverts p, and inverts μ. Ainf.lean:89–95 gives μ=[ε]−1, and ThetaKernel.lean:159–160 identifies ξ as a generator of ker θ. Colmez III.2 constructs A_max by convergent restricted series in ξ/p and allows any generator of ker θ. His B_max is A_max[1/p,1/t]. Lemma III.3.9 proves t/([ε]−1) is a unit of A_max, including at p=2, so the final localizations agree. Colmez defines the divided-power ring B_cris separately. III.4 identifies its G_K-invariants with those of B_max after tensoring with a finite-dimensional continuous p-adic representation. Carrying this comparison to general modules and filters in the compact development needs another argument.
sources: P. Colmez, Théorie d’Iwasawa des représentations de de Rham d’un corps local, Annals of Mathematics 148 (1998), §III.2, §III.3 Lemma III.3.9 and §III.4, pp. 24–29 in the author's copy

BdR.exists_sub_mem_of_smul_sub_mem.verdict: A filtered consequence of the degree-zero parts of Tate's two theorems.
BdR.exists_sub_mem_of_smul_sub_mem.comparison: Let K be the fixed field of the open image j(Γ) in G_p, S any B_dR⁺-submodule of B_dR and x∈B_dR. If g x−x∈S for every g∈j(Γ), there is an a∈K with x−a∈S. Tate §3.3 gives C_p^G_K=K. For each nonzero power of χ the extension cut out by the character is a totally ramified Z_p-extension after finite base change, so his Theorem 2 gives C_p(n)^G_K=0 for n≠0. Colmez III.1 identifies B_dR⁺ as a discrete valuation ring with residue C_p and uniformizer t transforming by χ. A proper nonzero submodule of its fraction field is t^m B_dR⁺ for some integer m. If x lies outside S, its leading term below the cutoff is fixed in gr^n≃C_p(n), and hence must have degree zero. Subtract its residue a∈K. A remaining nonzero leading term below the cutoff would have positive degree, which is impossible. The same argument without a cutoff covers S=0, and S=B_dR is immediate. Only H⁰ of the two Tate theorems enters.
sources: J. Tate, p-Divisible Groups, Proceedings of a Conference on Local Fields (1967), §3.3, Theorems 1 and 2, p. 176
P. Colmez, Théorie d’Iwasawa des représentations de de Rham d’un corps local, §III.1, B_dR⁺, its residue and the action on t

CMLattice.complex_multiplication_theta.verdict: The cited CM reciprocity theorem identifies the action on torsion. Equality of the full, normalized translated theta germs needs a further comparison.
CMLattice.complex_multiplication_theta.comparison: K=ℚ(√−d) with d prime and d≡7 mod 8. C is a marked CM datum with Λ_C=Ω₀𝒪_K and σ∈Aut(ℂ/K). D is a datum chosen to satisfy a₁(D)=σ(a₁(C)). Lean produces Ω∈ℂˣ with area(D)=|Ω|²√d/2, a positive integer e with eΩ∈Λ_D, and scalars a(S)∈K for every finite subset S of K. Their diagonal images have a cluster point β in the finite adèles along finite subsets ordered by inclusion. For every such S and x∈S, applying σ to every Taylor coefficient at zero of U_{xΩ₀}θ_C gives the coefficients of U_{xΩa(S)}θ_D. The class of β under reciprocity, invertibility of β, and convergence to β are absent from the conclusion. Shimura 5.4 instead specifies an idèle s lifting σ by reciprocity and a unique compatible uniformization; s⁻¹ gives the action on all torsion. Milne 9.17 gives the polarized uniformization version. Lifting this torsion statement to the project's normalized translate of the sigma section requires control of the invariant differential, automorphy factors and scalar or root of unity in each translated section, consistently for each finite S. Bannai–Kobayashi 2.9 gives a field of definition for the Taylor coefficients of torsion translates under explicit rationality and divisor-normalization hypotheses, and their proof tracks a root of unity. It does not by itself identify the two particular normalized germs and the simultaneous finite-set multipliers in Lean. The pinned intermediate exists_taylorVia_twistedTranslate_theta supplies that equality inside the development.
sources: G. Shimura, Introduction to the Arithmetic Theory of Automorphic Functions (1971), §5.3, Theorem 5.4, p. 117 (right page of scan), with the torsion diagram and the inverse idèle explicitly shown.
J. S. Milne, Complex Multiplication, v0.10 (2020), II §9, Theorem 9.17, pp. 80–81, finite idèle, type of the conjugate and torsion diagram.

K. Bannai and S. Kobayashi, Algebraic theta functions and the p-adic interpolation of Eisenstein–Kronecker numbers, §2.2, Theorem 2.9, pp. 25–26 in arXiv v4, and Theorem 2.12, pp. 26–27, for the translated sigma expansion.
Pinned σ, chosen conjugate, and equality of translated Taylor series on a finite set, ConjugateCurve.lean 11 and 69–81.
Pinned Taylor coefficient convention and normalized twisted theta, CurveTheta.lean 65–69 and 100–112.

CMLattice.exists_unit_coeff_degree_le.verdict: The unit-coefficient bound follows from the inseparable degree of the reduced isogeny, after identifying the integral local parameter.
CMLattice.exists_unit_coeff_degree_le.comparison: Fix a marked CM datum for prime d≡7 mod 8, any prime p and embedding into ℂₚ. Z has constant coefficient 0 and linear coefficient 1. Substitution f(Z) has integral coefficients for all f∈𝔬[[φ]]. Multiplication by a carries Λ into itself and aā=q with q an odd natural number. The series g is integral, has zero constant term, and satisfies Z(g(T))=ιₚ(a)Z(T). The literal conclusion negates the statement that all coefficients in degrees ≤q have norm different from 1, so the reduction of g has a nonzero term in some degree 1 through q. On the smooth normalized cubic the function φ is a parameter at the marked origin: φ(0)=0 and φ′(0)=1. Hence u(T)=φ(Z(T)) is integral by the hypothesis and has an integral compositional inverse. In the u-coordinate the identity for g is the formal action of the analytic isogeny z↦az, using translation to the marked point. The integral model has unit discriminant by the pinned norm_disc_eq_one. After descending the cubic and isogeny to a number field and specializing at the chosen place, Silverman II.4.4 in Advanced Topics preserves degree q. His Arithmetic IV.7.2 and IV.7.4 give the first nonzero reduced degree as p^height, equal to the inseparable degree, which is ≤q. The integral coordinate change preserves this order. The Lean declaration asks for the bound alone, for odd q; it supplies neither a specified exponent nor an isomorphism class of a formal module. Drinfel'd Proposition 1.7 instead classifies formal 𝒪-modules of a given finite height over a separably closed residue field.
sources: J. H. Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, 2nd ed., IV §7, Proposition 7.2(a,b), p. 133, Theorem 7.4 and Corollary 7.5, p. 134. The order of a nonzero formal isogeny is p^height, and for an elliptic isogeny equals its inseparable degree.
J. H. Silverman, Advanced Topics in the Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, II §4, Proposition 4.4, pp. 124–126, for injectivity and preservation of isogeny degree at good reduction.
V. G. Drinfel'd, Elliptic modules (1974), §1(D), Proposition 1.7, pp. 566–567, finite-height classification and the endomorphism algebra.
Pinned derivative of φ and the normalized Weierstrass equation, CurveTheta.lean 310–321.
Pinned IsIsogeny as lattice inclusion and an area/degree equality, SigmaFunction.lean 47–50.

CMLattice.norm_a₁_le_one.verdict: Integrality of this specified coefficient follows from CM integrality of j and the equation of the marked cubic.
CMLattice.norm_a₁_le_one.comparison: Fix a rational prime d≡7 mod 8, a CM period lattice C with its marked point t and normalized a₁, a prime p, and a field embedding ιₚ:ℂ→ℂₚ. The structure requires 2t∈Λ, t∉Λ, stability under 𝒪_K for K=ℚ(√−d), the two marked nonmembership conditions, g₂=12℘(t)²−4 and a₁²=12℘(t). The conclusion is |ιₚ(a₁)|≤1. The pinned functions satisfy y²+a₁xy=x³+x. Its standard invariants are c₄=a₁⁴−48 and Δ=a₁⁴−64. Since j=c₄³/Δ is a CM singular modulus, it is an algebraic integer. Thus a₁ satisfies the monic polynomial (T⁴−48)³−j(T⁴−64), giving the claimed integrality at every p-adic embedding. This derivation uses the normalization of the cubic. The stronger pinned lemma norm_disc_eq_one proves |ιₚ(a₁⁴−64)|=1 and supplies the actual Lean one-line proof by adding 64. The local declaration concludes only coefficient integrality. No identification with a particular Weber unit is required for this conclusion.
sources: M. Deuring, Die Klassenkörper der komplexen Multiplikation (1958), English translation by C.-W. Chin, §13, p. 31 of the translation, explicitly uses integrality of the singular class invariant j(α).
D. A. Cox, Primes of the Form x²+ny², §11, Theorem 11.1, p. 220, gives integrality for j of a proper fractional ideal of an imaginary quadratic order.

J. H. Silverman, Advanced Topics in the Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, II §6, Theorem 6.1, p. 140, CM j-integrality; the Weierstrass invariant formulae are in The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, 2nd ed., III §1, p. 42.
Pinned data and the equation of the normalized cubic, CurveTheta.lean 81–92 and 307–321.

CMLattice.one_le_norm_coeff_translatedWp.verdict: The premise detects vanishing of the Hasse invariant and accounts for nonsplitting. The second-kind coefficient estimate requires a separate calculation.
CMLattice.one_le_norm_coeff_translatedWp.comparison: For a marked CM datum C with prime d≡7 mod 8, an arbitrary prime p, and the chosen embedding into ℂₚ, the hypothesis concerns every f in 𝔬[[φ]], where ξ(z)=℘(z+t)−℘(t) and φ=(℘′(z+t)−a₁ξ)/2. It requires |[z^(p−1)]f′|<1. The two conclusions are |[z^(p−1)]ιₚ(ξ)|≥1 and χ_K(p)≠1, which allows an inert or ramified p. For the normalized cubic, invariant differentiation D=d/dz preserves 𝔬[[φ]] and Dφ(0)=1. The expression tested is D^p f(0)/(p−1)!, with denominator a p-adic unit. In the reduction, D^p=A·D by Katz–Mazur, so testing f=φ forces the Hasse invariant A to vanish. This gives supersingular reduction. Its rational endomorphism algebra at p is a division quaternion algebra. Specialization embeds K into the rational endomorphism algebra, so splitting would embed ℚₚ×ℚₚ into a division algebra, contradicting the absence of nontrivial idempotents. Silverman V.4.1(a) computes a Hasse invariant for y²=f(x) in odd residue characteristic from [x^(p−1)]f(x)^((p−1)/2). That coefficient is a different expression from the displayed coefficient of the analytically translated ℘-function. The pinned proof rules out p=2 in the premise and proves its lower bound by a recurrence among derivatives and powers of ξ. The general Hasse and CM reduction statements do not supply that recurrence or an equivalent published coefficient comparison.
sources: N. Katz and B. Mazur, Arithmetic Moduli of Elliptic Curves (1985), §12.4.1, especially (12.4.1.1) and (12.4.1.3), p. 354, for the Hasse coefficient of [p] and the restricted p-th power of the invariant derivation.
N. Katz, p-adic properties of modular schemes and modular forms, §2.0, pp. 97–98, gives the p-th iterate description of Frobenius on the invariant derivation.

M. Deuring, Die Typen der Multiplikatorenringe elliptischer Funktionenkörper, Abh. Math. Sem. Hansischen Univ. 14 (1941), introduction nos. 2–3, pp. 198–200; §11 no. 1, pp. 269–270, relates reduction to splitting in the CM field.

J. H. Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, 2nd ed., V §3, Theorem 3.1(a), pp. 144–145, and V §4, Theorem 4.1(a), pp. 148–149 (equivalent supersingularity criteria and the characteristic-p cubic coefficient formula).
Pinned derivative in the integral formal parameter, IntegralParameter.lean 81–96 and 280–305.
Pinned coefficient recurrence and Legendre-symbol implication, FormalHeight.lean 137–162.

DiscreteModule.FiniteKilledFixedInj.isHi.verdict: An explicit relative-trace witness from an invertible subgroup index on the coefficient module.
DiscreteModule.FiniteKilledFixedInj.isHi.comparison: Let d=[G:Q]. Bézout gives an integer b with bd≡1 mod n. Set τ=b·id on A. Every conjugate of τ equals τ, so the sum over cosets is bd·id=id on the n-torsion module. The input package also asserts that A is finite, Q acts trivially and ρ(z)−m is injective; the construction uses the torsion and coprimality conditions. The result asserts the additive trace witness under the project's definition. The equivalence with relative projectivity of a finite-group representation over a field is the larger classical criterion. G itself in the Lean declaration need only have finitely many Q-cosets.
sources: Aschbacher, Kessar and Oliver, Fusion Systems in Algebra and Topology, representation-theory appendix, Theorem 4.2 (Higman's criterion), relative trace of the identity

Filling.exists_big_cell_decomp.verdict: Bruhat cells over a field are classical. An exact reference identifying these minors, unipotents and intermediate floor factors remains open.
Filling.exists_big_cell_decomp.comparison: A is a field with involution and an element of trace one, and T.splitGram is invertible and Hermitian. For γ in its isometry group assume every leading minor of the frame Gram matrix is nonzero. For every floor j, including the default top floor ϱ, the theorem gives u,u′ in the Bessel unipotent, units p_i and σ in GT(j), with γ=u⁻¹w_j(p)σu′. The element w_j(p) exchanges the first j hyperbolic pairs with reciprocal conjugate scalings. GT(j) fixes the preceding pairs, and at the top the middle isometry group remains. Borel–Tits §5.15 decomposes the rational points of a connected reductive group into U(k)nU(k) and gives the product coordinates of each cell. Knapp gives the real Lie group version. To identify this exact result one still needs the field and form hypotheses for the relevant group, the frame-minor criterion selecting the cell and the truncation at each j for this particular Bessel radical. The source supplies the latter by successively eliminating hyperbolic pairs.
sources: A. Borel and J. Tits, Groupes réductifs, Publications Mathématiques de l’IHÉS 27 (1965), §§5.13–5.15, especially Théorème 5.15, pp. 99–101
A. Knapp, Structure theory of semisimple Lie groups, Theorem 4.9, Bruhat decomposition, and its reference to Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Theorem 7.40

HCParam.HasLargeGap.isUnitaryCasimirGe_d.verdict: Orthogonality explains the evaluation bound after identifying the concrete coefficient model. The additional Casimir assertion and the model identification need separate evidence.
HCParam.HasLargeGap.isUnitaryCasimirGe_d.comparison: For nonempty n and a Harish–Chandra parameter l=2λ with distinct entries of the prescribed parity and opposite-sign gaps at least 500n³+A in λ, D_λ is generated from a specific normalized Flensted–Jensen integral ψ by complexified right derivatives. It has the inner product induced by the source's map into L². The conclusion includes the adjoint identity for E_ab with sign ε_aε_b, the Casimir estimate Re⟨y,Ωy⟩≥(|λ|²−|ρ|²)‖y‖², ‖ψ‖=1 and |y(g)|≤‖y‖ at every point. CasimirBound.lean:18–21 supplies the numerical clause. Duflo–Moore's orthogonality for an irreducible square-integrable representation of a unimodular group relates Haar norms of its coefficients to the Hilbert norm by its formal degree. For a unit vector, pointwise evaluation of its coefficient satisfies the Cauchy–Schwarz bound. That theorem presupposes the unitary model. It does not identify this integral and its right-derivative module, their normalization, or the Casimir scalar. Those constitute the outstanding comparison to the catalogue's Schur citation.
sources: Harish-Chandra, Representations of semisimple Lie groups VI, American Journal of Mathematics 78 (1956), §3, Schur orthogonality relations
M. Duflo and C. Moore, On the regular representation of a nonunimodular locally compact group, Journal of Functional Analysis 21 (1976), Theorem 3, orthogonality relations
C. Moore, Square integrable primary representations, Pacific Journal of Mathematics 70 (1977), pp. 413–415, unimodular and irreducible cases and explicit orthogonality identity

IsAdmissible.of_jointly_injective.verdict: Fontaine proves subobject stability in the finite-dimensional representation category. The compact filter and module generality remains unlocated.
IsAdmissible.of_jointly_injective.comparison: RegularityFrobenius.lean:21–29 supplies the parameters of the one-line header. The homomorphism j from an abstract group Γ has open image in G_p. Every member of F contains the pullback of a neighbourhood of 1. There are finitely many jointly injective Z_p-linear maps from T′ to the S_i, with each map intertwining the actions on all vectors for F-almost every g. Spanning by F-fixed periods in B_max⊗S_i then implies spanning in B_max⊗T′. Source and targets may use different compatible coefficient algebras. None of these modules is required to have finite rank. Fontaine III, Proposition 1.5.2, gives closure of finite-dimensional B-admissible representations under genuine subobjects, with the usual exact fibre functor. The finite product followed by inclusion works in that category. Extending the argument to eventual equivariance, this filter and arbitrary modules is the missing published comparison.
sources: J.-M. Fontaine, Représentations p-adiques semi-stables, Astérisque 223, Exposé III (1994), §§1.5.1–1.5.3, Proposition 1.5.2, pp. 124–125
O. Brinon and B. Conrad, CMI Summer School Notes on p-adic Hodge Theory, Theorem 5.2.1, the finite-dimensional B-admissible category

IsAdmissible.of_pairing.verdict: The classical dual and Tate-twist rules explain the field-valued case. The complete filtered-ring assertion remains unlocated.
IsAdmissible.of_pairing.comparison: Here j has open image and every F-set contains the pullback of a neighbourhood of 1. T is finite free over a commutative Z_p-algebra R. An R-linear isomorphism b identifies the σ-module T″ with Hom_R(T,R) and satisfies b(σ(g)x)(ρ(g)y)=χ(g)^c b(x)(y), for an integer c. From F-admissibility of ρ one gets F-admissibility of σ. For each inertia Weil pair (j(s),0), every polynomial over R killing β_{ρ,s,0} also kills β_{σ,s⁻¹,0}. The predicate includes potential crystallinity. For finite-dimensional continuous p-adic representations Fontaine III gives tensor and dual admissibility. Colmez III.4 computes twists, whose associated Weil inertia is trivial, and Fontaine VIII §2.3.7 gives the Weil action. Duality at s⁻¹ then transposes the original inertia action and preserves the same annihilating polynomial. Extending these statements to F, arbitrary R and its finite free modules needs a further source or argument.
sources: J.-M. Fontaine, Représentations p-adiques semi-stables, Exposé III, §1.5, Proposition 1.5.2
P. Colmez, Théorie d’Iwasawa des représentations de de Rham d’un corps local, §III.4, formula for D_cris(V(k))
J.-M. Fontaine, Représentations ℓ-adiques potentiellement semi-stables, Exposé VIII, §2.3.7, Weil action

IsAutFunction.apply_eq_apply_one.verdict: Constancy follows from strong approximation for the special unitary group together with the stated torus hypothesis.
IsAutFunction.apply_eq_apply_one.comparison: Kneser's Satz 2 gives density away from a set with a noncompact factor for the simply connected almost-simple classical group SU(W). The specified hyperbolic line makes SU(W) isotropic at every place, and S contains a finite place. For any fixed g, the continuous function h ↦ D(hg) on SU(W)(A) is invariant under rational elements on the left and under the full special unitary factor over a place in S on the right, since conjugation by g preserves that local subgroup. Density makes this function constant. This gives left invariance under SU(W)(A), hence under the unipotent radical. The additional hypothesis now removes the line-torus coordinate on the Levi. Every norm-one adelic determinant is t/t̄ by idelic Hilbert 90. The line Levi acts by t on one isotropic line and t̄⁻¹ on its dual, so each element agrees in determinant with such a Levi element. This proves D(g)=D(1). The given integral level away from S is compatible with the argument. Kneser applies to SU(W), and the torus premise supplies the passage to U(W).
sources: Kneser, Starke Approximation in algebraischen Gruppen I, §1, (1.1), (1.4) and Satz 2, pp. 190–191
Harari, Galois Cohomology and Class Field Theory, Theorem 6.5 (Hilbert 90) and Proposition 13.1(b) (idèle cohomology as the sum of local groups)
Pinned block action of the Levi on the hyperbolic pair

IsDualFamily.eq_zero_of_coeff.verdict: Compact-quotient Fourier uniqueness with an explicit reduction to the compatible characters.
IsDualFamily.eq_zero_of_coeff.comparison: For a continuous periodic F, Lean requires the vanishing of the mean of χ_i F only at those i for which every identity c F(x+a)=F(x) implies χ_i(a)=c. At every other i, translation invariance of the mean forces the coefficient to vanish, since it is multiplied by two different scalars. The character family contains constants, separates points of the compact quotient and is closed under multiplication and conjugation. Its span is dense by Stone–Weierstrass. Vanishing of the coefficients therefore forces the measure F times Haar measure to vanish and continuity gives F=0 pointwise. The classical uniqueness theorem applies after this reduction.
sources: Rudin, Fourier Analysis on Groups, §1.3, Theorem 1.3.6 (uniqueness), p. 17

IsDualFamily.sum_le_of_fourier.verdict: A one-sided Poisson estimate for a nonnegative integrable function, with local lower semicontinuity replacing global regularity.
IsDualFamily.sum_le_of_fourier.comparison: Lean bounds a finite sum of point values by S when every finite partial sum of absolute Fourier coefficients on the dual rational lattice is ≤S. The number field is totally complex. Only the points in the specified finite set need lower semicontinuity. Tate's Theorem 4.1.4 identifies the annihilator of the rational lattice. The Poisson identity is Lemma 4.2.4. Its continuity and uniform periodization hypotheses do not hold for the general Lean input. To pass to the inequality, integrate the periodization on the compact quotient against a nonnegative approximate identity at zero. Its Fourier coefficients are at most one in modulus, and absolute summability bounds the averaged sum by S. Nonnegativity and lower semicontinuity at the finitely many points give the desired lower limit. This proves the comparison after smoothing and preserves the normalized Haar covolume.
sources: Tate, Fourier Analysis in Number Fields and Hecke's Zeta-Functions, Theorem 4.1.4, Lemmas 4.2.1–4.2.4 and the normalization following Theorem 4.2.1

IsHCParam.prod_formalDegree.verdict: The compact formal-degree identity is Schur orthogonality with probability Haar measure. The right side is a tableau-model dimension.
IsHCParam.prod_formalDegree.comparison: For finite Φ,n, each l_w reorders twice the Harish-Chandra parameter of the algebraic weight (κ_w,e_w). In zero-based descending order its p-th entry is 2(e_w+Σ_{p<h<|n|}κ_w(h))+|n|−1−2p. All signs are positive. HCParam.formalDegree is the inverse integral of |dsCoeff|². WeightParameter.lean:60–66 identifies the product of the conjugate coefficients with the coefficient of the unit highest vector in the tensor product of the corresponding conjugated Schur modules with determinant twists. Knapp, Corollary 6.29(b), gives integral 1/dim for such a vector and Haar mass one. Product integration gives the product of local formal degrees. In this model each coordinate is indexed by a family of standard fillings in WeylIndex n κ, so the dimension is their cardinality. The statement itself contains no Weyl alternant or product of positive-root ratios. The determinant twists leave the dimension unchanged.
sources: A. W. Knapp, Advanced Real Analysis, digital second edition, Chapter VI, Corollary 6.29(b), p. 249, Schur orthogonality for normalized Haar measure
Compact-group and polynomial-representation notes hosted by N. Wallach, Theorems 4.5 and 10.7, especially the Schur-character description of irreducible GL modules

IsHolOfWeight.integral_mul_conj_holMinor.verdict: The usual Hilbert-space reproducing property is located. The product and integrability hypotheses in this formula require more.
IsHolOfWeight.integral_mul_conj_holMinor.comparison: For a finite product of copies of U(diag ε), the order o is injective with all positive-sign indices first. Each factor weight u_τ is dominant within the two compact blocks. IsHolOfWeight means that F extends analytically to the products hb for upper-triangular b in the o order, with the given diagonal character. Define m as the product of the normalized quotients of principal minors in RepresentationDefs.lean:171–183. Assuming F·conj(m) is integrable for the compact-dual Haar measure, the integral equals (∫|m|²)F(1). The declaration imposes neither square integrability of F nor a holomorphic-discrete-series gap on u. Korányi's §4, (4.1), is the reproducing identity for vectors in an actual Hilbert space of holomorphic sections, and (4.4)–(4.5) characterize its equivariant kernel. To use it here one must identify its evaluation vector with the explicit m, transfer the measures and justify evaluation under just mixed-product integrability, including parameters outside the discrete-series range. The Lean proof uses its own circle-average identity at lines 45–51.
sources: A. Korányi, A simplified approach to the holomorphic discrete series, Indagationes Mathematicae 35 (2024), §4, formulas (4.1) and (4.4)–(4.5), and §6, condition (6.4)

Harish-Chandra, Representations of semisimple Lie groups V, American Journal of Mathematics 78 (1956), §§4–5 and §9 on holomorphic function spaces and unitarity. The exact compact minors identity remains unlocated.

IsMatch.exists_isJointHarmonic.verdict: The unitary compact-type correspondence and its minimal-degree formula give the strong harmonic highest vector for the matched parameters.
IsMatch.exists_isJointHarmonic.comparison: In the signed rectangular Fock model suppose l,l′ satisfy the gaps and the centred row–column matching of OscillatorDefs.lean:124–131. The sought polynomial is nonzero, highest of both prescribed lowest K-types, and every mixed second derivative in a column across opposite-sign rows, or in a row across opposite-sign columns, vanishes separately. The usual harmonicity equations use sums of these derivatives. To compare weights, subtract each vacuum weight. For a row of sign a this is γ−n′/2+σa(r−s)/2, with r,s the column sign counts. Dualizing the column action gives the corresponding primed formula. The two common scalar shifts are determinant twists on the covers, and σ exchanges column-sign labels. In JointHarmonicUnique.lean:77–96 and JointHarmonicExists.lean:69–84, each nonzero relative row weight pairs injectively with a column of the required sign, with the negative relative weight there. Every nonzero relative column weight occurs this way. Within a sign block the dominant order sorts the two positive and negative partitions. These are precisely the four partition lists and the two capacity conditions of Paul–Trapa (3.3)–(3.4), after taking the dual column highest weight in the opposite order. Thus the indicated tensor type occurs, with a nonzero joint highest vector by Howe §3. The homogeneous degree is the sum of absolute row relative weights by Paul–Trapa (3.6), and equally the column sum. In every monomial of that weight, its signed row degree equals the relative row weight. Equality in the sum of the triangle inequalities forbids simultaneous positive and negative variables in any row. The same argument for columns gives every individual mixed-derivative vanishing. With an empty side the weights are the vacuum weights and the constant polynomial suffices.
sources: R. Howe, Transcending classical invariant theory, JAMS 2 (1989), §3, Lemmas 3.2–3.3, homogeneous degree and irreducibility of the joint harmonic summand
A. Paul and P. Trapa, One-dimensional representations of U(p,q) and the Howe correspondence, §3, Lemma 3.2(1)–(2), especially formulas (3.3), (3.4) and (3.6), pp. 8–9 in the authors' copy

IsMatch.unique.verdict: Howe's multiplicity-free compact-pair correspondence implies proportionality for this one matched row type.
IsMatch.unique.comparison: Fix a rectangular Fock polynomial model with signed row and column sets and two central shifts. The two parameters have gaps 500(n+n′)³ and satisfy the centred matching condition of OscillatorDefs.lean:124–131. Each nonzero polynomial in the hypotheses is killed by the summed row and column Laplacians, has the prescribed compact highest row weight Λ, and is killed by the compact column raising operators. No column weight is specified in IsPreJointHarmonic. In the usual Fock model for U(p,q)×U(r,s), the degree-lowering invariant quadratic operators contract opposite-sign variables over one fixed row or column block. The two ordered versions of T.fockLaplacian for opposite signs give these two block contractions, and T.swap gives the contractions in the other direction. Relabelling variables, interchanging the column signs for the opposite polarization, taking the dual column action, and adding determinant characters on the covers preserve these kernels and highest lines. Howe §3, Lemma 3.3, shows that a fixed row type σ in joint harmonics has a unique companion σ′ and its summand is an irreducible σ⊗σ′ with multiplicity one. The highest line in σ and the subspace killed by all raising operators in σ′ both have dimension one. Thus P and Q lie on one line. Empty row or column sets reduce to constant polynomials.
sources: R. Howe, Transcending classical invariant theory, JAMS 2 (1989), §2 on the Fock model and §3, Lemma 3.3, (3.15) and the irreducibility and mutual-commutant assertions following it, pp. 543–544
A. Paul and P. Trapa, One-dimensional representations of U(p,q) and the Howe correspondence, §3, Theorem 3.1 and Lemma 3.2, compact type correspondence for unitary pairs

IsPlaceOver.exists_localArtin_eq.verdict: Existence in the image of local reciprocity with a specified valuation, after translating geometric Frobenius
IsPlaceOver.exists_localArtin_eq.comparison: Fix a number field K, w finite, a place A of the closure over w, and the project's topological pro-Galois group Γ acting on that closure. For n natural (including zero) and q=(Nw)^n the literal hypothesis IsFrob A q g⁻¹ says that g⁻¹ acts as the qth power on residues. The output x in K_w^× has v(x)=exp(−n) and geometric Artin image [g] in the abelianized decomposition group. As v(π)=exp(−1), the ordinary additive order of this x is +n. Serre takes arithmetic Frobenius F, uniformizers mapping to F on the unramified quotient, and identifies units with abelian inertia. Taking the inverse reciprocity map recovers the Lean normalization. The catalogue's arithmetic s and additive order −n give an equivalent formulation upon taking s=g⁻¹ and replacing x by x⁻¹. Its order and Frobenius are not the literal x and g of the declaration. Serre's isomorphism with the subgroup of integral Frobenius degree supplies existence. The Lean conclusion only selects a preimage with its degree and expresses the result through A and Γ.
sources: J.-P. Serre, Local Fields, XIII §4, Proposition 13 and corollary, pp. 197–198, and XIV §6, Theorem 1, Corollary 2 and Remark 2, pp. 218–219. The map on the unramified quotient is F raised to the additive valuation. The modified abelian group allows the integral powers of F.

IsPlaceOver.exists_localArtin_eq_tameGen.verdict: A simultaneous unit lift and primitive residue derived from two local reciprocity assertions
IsPlaceOver.exists_localArtin_eq_tameGen.comparison: For A over the finite place w of K in the Galois closure setup, the project chooses an inertia element γ whose Kummer action has exact order n on a suitable uniformizer radical for every n prime to the residue characteristic. Lean produces a single u in K_w^×, together with proof it is an integral unit, such that its geometric local Artin image equals the class of this particular γ, every residue-field unit is an integral power of its reduction, and v(u)=1. This does not prescribe which primitive residue to use. Surjectivity from units onto abelian inertia gives the first condition. To obtain the second for the same lift, apply the prime-to-p Kummer formula to a (Nw−1)st root of a uniformizer. Serre's arithmetic symbol for (π,u) gives the inverse residue for n=Nw−1. Inversion of reciprocity in Lean gives the residue of u, and the chosen generator forces its exact order Nw−1. This use of the tame symbol is essential even after unit surjectivity.
sources: J.-P. Serre, Local Fields, XIII §4, Proposition 13 and its corollary, pp. 197–198, and XIV §6, Corollary 2(ii), p. 219. Units and inertia in the abelian reciprocity map.
Serre, Local Fields, XIV §2, Proposition 6, p. 208, and §3, Proposition 8 with finite-field corollary, pp. 210–211. The first identifies the Kummer ratio, the second computes its residue.
Pinned choice of γ and its use at n=Nw−1, ArtinMapAtPlace.lean, lines 234–276.

IsPolar.landau.verdict: corollary of Widder II.5b with a residue argument and a measurable density
IsPolar.landau.comparison: Let E be real measurable and r complex-valued on C. IsPolar E r means there are a real C and a globally meromorphic Φ with |E(v)| ≤ C exp(v) for v ≥ 0, Φ(s) = ∫₀^∞ E(v) exp((1−s)v) dv for Re s > 2, and (s−1)Φ(s) analytic near every point of Re s ≥ 1. At every ρ with Re ρ > 0 the punctured limit of (s−ρ)Φ(s) is r(ρ). Suppose β > 0, Re r(x) ≥ 0 at every real x > β, and E(v) ≤ exp((β−1)v) eventually. Lean concludes r(ρ) = 0 for every complex ρ with Re ρ > β. Choose K large enough that g(v) = K exp(βv) − E(v) exp(v) is nonnegative on v ≥ 0. Local boundedness and measurability make its indefinite integral nondecreasing and locally absolutely continuous, as required for Widder’s Laplace–Stieltjes theorem. Its transform continues as Ψ(s) = K/(s−β) − Φ(s). If its real abscissa a exceeded β, Widder would force a singularity at a. Meromorphy and the finite residue limit allow at most a simple pole there. Positivity along the real axis makes its residue real and nonnegative, while its value −r(a) has nonpositive real part, so that singularity is removable. The transform is therefore holomorphic on Re s > β and all the asserted residues vanish. Montgomery–Vaughan use a locally Riemann-integrable density. Lean assumes only measurability and supplies the bound needed for the Stieltjes formulation.
sources: D. V. Widder, The Laplace Transform, Chapter II, §5, Theorem 5b, p. 58. The 1946 second printing of the 1941 edition specifies a finite abscissa and a monotone determining function.
H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan, Multiplicative Number Theory I, §15.1, Lemma 15.1, p. 463. The locally Riemann-integrable formulation for a density of eventual constant sign.

IsPotCrys.exists_hasJumps.verdict: The transition from potential crystallinity to Hodge–Tate weights is classical for field coefficients. The arbitrary coefficient-fibre formulation remains unlocated.
IsPotCrys.exists_hasJumps.comparison: Assume j:Γ→G_p has open image, R is a commutative Z_p-algebra, T is finite free over R with compatible Z_p action, and its periods fixed near 1 span B_max⊗T. For every Z_p-algebra map γ:R→C_p there is a multiset J with cardinality rank_R(T). For each u its multiplicity is the Q̄_p-dimension of γ-semilinear functions f:T→C_p with f(ρ(g)x)=χ(g)^(−u)j(g)f(x) near 1 for each x. Defs.lean:88–101 does not require γ to be injective. Fontaine III §5.1.7 places crystalline representations inside de Rham representations. Theorem 3.8(i) and Remark 3.9(ii) identify the Hodge–Tate grading and descend the Hodge–Tate or de Rham condition from a finite extension. These are statements about finite-dimensional continuous p-adic representations of G_K. A passage to the arbitrary ring R, all its γ and the pointwise eventual semilinear functions still needs justification.
sources: J.-M. Fontaine, Représentations p-adiques semi-stables, Exposé III, Theorem 3.8(i), Remark 3.9(ii) and §5.1.7, pp. 142–143 and 157–158

IsPotCrys.isCrystalline_of_inertia_fixes.verdict: Unramified descent and Weil inertia account for the classical crystalline criterion. The arbitrary-module descent remains unlocated.
IsPotCrys.isCrystalline_of_inertia_fixes.comparison: The ring R is any commutative Z_p-algebra and T is an R-module with compatible Z_p action. For j:Γ→G_p of open image assume that fixed periods near 1 span B_max⊗T, and β_{s,0}=1 for every s with j(s) in inertia. The conclusion is that periods fixed by every g in Γ span B_max⊗T. The inertia hypothesis concerns the linear action on periods. It need not say that inertia acts trivially on T. For a finite-dimensional potentially crystalline G_K-representation, Fontaine's D_pcris is the union of period modules over finite extensions, with N=0. The Weil inertia action is ordinary descent inertia on these periods. If it is trivial, periods descend through the unramified part by Galois descent, giving D_cris of full dimension. Fontaine's comparison and descent are formulated in the finite-dimensional category. A published argument for arbitrary T and the compact B_max-spanning definition is missing.
sources: J.-M. Fontaine, Représentations p-adiques semi-stables, Exposé III, §§1.8.5–1.8.6 and §5.6.8(iii), unramified descent and potentially crystalline periods
J.-M. Fontaine, Représentations ℓ-adiques potentiellement semi-stables, Exposé VIII, §§2.3.2–2.3.3 and §2.3.7
O. Brinon and B. Conrad, CMI Summer School Notes on p-adic Hodge Theory, Proposition 9.3.1, invariance under unramified extension

IsPotCrys.relIndex_dvd_of_orthogonal.verdict: Finite Tate duality and the Bloch–Kato finite condition explain separate inputs to the integral cochain divisibility
IsPotCrys.relIndex_dvd_of_orthogonal.comparison: Let ℓ be prime, R a p-adic integer ring at ℓ, Γ a topological group with an open embedding into G_ℓ, and L,L′ potentially crystalline Galois lattices over R. The perfect ℤ_ℓ-linear pairing on L′ × L takes its equivariance twist from the cyclotomic character. Take any m≥0 and an equivariant surjective ℤ_ℓ-linear map q:L→V with kernel ℓ^mL, V finite discrete. Write A=q(Z_f(L)). Here Z_f consists of maps whose period extension is a coboundary for every group element. The Lean period ring called Bcris is Colmez's B_max. For additive subgroups H of maps Γ→L′ and S of maps Γ→V, A∪S must consist of continuous 1-cocycles. Each s in A∪S has a function lift a via q such that, for every c in H, (g,h)↦ζ of the residue mod ℓ^m of b(g·c(h),a(g)) is a multiplicative 2-coboundary in the algebraic closure of ℚ_ℓ. H and the chosen lifts are not separately assumed to consist of continuous cocycles. The output is [S:S∩A] dividing [Z_f(L′):H∩Z_f(L′)]. Milne's finite duality pairs cohomology classes and his Euler characteristic counts H⁰,H¹,H². Bloch–Kato prove finite-local-condition annihilators on rational cohomology, and on a lattice paired with its divisible dual, under the de Rham hypothesis at ℓ. Their dimension formula is rational. Comparison of the period condition with B_max, quotient and coboundary sizes, and finite-level passage to these arbitrary cochain subgroups are additional steps. The project proves its own dual cocycle order formula in lines 48–54 and uses it in lines 69–132. The cited classical places alone do not state the Lean divisibility.
sources: J. S. Milne, Arithmetic Duality Theorems, 2nd ed., I §2, Corollary 2.3, p. 28 (perfect finite local pairing), and Theorem 2.8, p. 31 (local Euler–Poincaré characteristic).

S. Bloch and K. Kato, L-functions and Tamagawa numbers of motives, The Grothendieck Festschrift I, §3.7, pp. 353–354, Proposition 3.8, p. 354, and Corollary 3.8.4, p. 355. The groups here are H¹ with the finite local condition.

J.-P. Serre, Galois Cohomology, II §§5.2 and 5.7, sections beginning on pp. 90 and 99. The accessible preview confirms these section titles and pages. The numerical statements above were checked in Milne's full text.
Pinned period-ring identification, BdR.lean, lines 4–8, and the associated cocycle definition in Crystalline/Defs.lean, lines 51–57.

IsTameExponent.pow_apply_charName.verdict: Prime-to-p norm residue reciprocity expressed in the project's faithful-character coordinates
IsTameExponent.pow_apply_charName.comparison: Let E be an embedded number field, w a finite place with residue size q, and K an algebraically closed extension of k_w with faithful multiplicative character T. IsTameExponent w A T f s a includes A over w, f≠0, s in inertia, and a residue embedding for which s(z)/z on a (q^f−1)st uniformizer radical has character exp(2πi/(q^f−1))^a. Given u of multiplicative valuation 1 whose geometric local Artin image equals the abelianized class of s, every residue-field multiplicative character χ satisfies (T^a)(xχ)=χ(ū) for its named element xχ. Restrict to the (q−1)st radical using q−1 | q^f−1. With arithmetic reciprocity Serre's formula gives the inverse residue for (π,u) at n=q−1; in the project's geometric normalization the Kummer ratio is ū. Applying the finite cyclic character duality defining xχ gives the displayed equality. Serre's formula does not use this choice of T or the name xχ.
sources: J.-P. Serre, Local Fields, XIV §2, Proposition 6, p. 208, and §3, Proposition 8 and finite-field corollary, pp. 210–211. The Kummer ratio computes the prime-to-p norm residue symbol, with arithmetic reciprocity.
Pinned tame exponent, character evaluation and use of localArtin_tame_symbol.

IsTraceNondeg.comp.verdict: The complete-reducibility part of Clifford's theorem, recast in characteristic-zero trace form
IsTraceNondeg.comp.comparison: Let k be algebraically closed of characteristic zero, G and H arbitrary groups, r:G→GL_n(k) with nondegenerate trace pairing on the span of r(G), and f:H→G with normal image. Clifford's Theorem 1 allows any ground field and any group and characterizes the restriction of each irreducible summand to a normal subgroup as a sum of conjugate simple constituents. Apply this to image f, take direct sums, and pull back along the surjection H→image f. Finite-dimensionality makes the matrix span Artinian. In characteristic zero its semisimple action has a nondegenerate trace form, block by block with positive integral multiplicities. Conversely a radical lies in the trace kernel. These facts translate the input and conclusion. Lean does not record the conjugacy or multiplicity of constituents.
sources: A. H. Clifford, Representations induced in an invariant subgroup, Ann. of Math. 38 (1937), §1, Theorem 1, pp. 534–535. Clifford uses “induced” here for restriction to H.

IsTraceNondeg.exists_conj_of_trace_eq.verdict: The characteristic-zero character criterion for semisimple representations after translating the two algebraic hypotheses
IsTraceNondeg.exists_conj_of_trace_eq.comparison: Over algebraically closed k of characteristic zero, let r:G→GL_n(k) have nondegenerate trace form on its span. Let ρ:G→B land in a finite-dimensional k-algebra with semiprime image span, and let φ:B→M_n(k) be a unital algebra map. If traces of r(g) and φρ(g) agree for every g, one invertible P intertwines them simultaneously. A finite-dimensional semiprime span is semisimple, its quotient through φ is semisimple, and the trace criterion gives semisimplicity for r. Extend trace equality linearly from G to its group algebra. Independence of the distinct simple characters in characteristic zero yields equal multiplicities and the claimed change of basis. Conversely putting B=M_n and taking the second semisimple representation as ρ recovers the familiar matrix form for arbitrary G. The 1941 paper's subject is finite groups in modular representation theory. The cited modern algebra theorem gives the exact generality needed here.
sources: R. Brauer and C. Nesbitt, On the modular characters of groups, Ann. of Math. 42 (1941), Part I, §§1, 3 and 6. The published setup starts with finite groups and studies ordinary and modular characters.

P. Etingof et al., Introduction to representation theory, §2.6, Theorem 2.17(i), p. 27, and the characteristic-zero multiplicity argument following Theorem 2.18, p. 28. Distinct irreducible characters of an associative algebra are linearly independent.
Pinned semiprime-span criterion and Wedderburn decomposition.

Isotypic.attached_galRep.verdict: Coefficientwise ℓ-adic approximation on the Frobenius filter follows from exact unramified compatibility after definite-unitary base change and decomposition of the discrete GL constituents.
Isotypic.attached_galRep.comparison: The rank n is positive, V is the standard definite unitary space over a CM field E, a prime ℓ and an isomorphism ℂ ≃ Q̄ℓ are fixed, and E has WeilData. This includes a primitive 5040th root of unity, the splitting character with its inert sign, an imaginary element satisfying the positivity and integrality conditions, and the finite self-duality idele. A nonzero algebraic form f in x has the chosen spherical eigenvalues at all but finitely many split w. AttachedDefs.lean:16–19 requires continuity, nondegeneracy of the trace pairing on the image algebra, openness of the identity map, and for every η>0 eventual coefficientwise distance ≤η on mostFrobenii. The last filter uses prime-norm w and passage to a smaller nonempty open subset of each nonempty open Galois set. An exact identity at cofinally many such w suffices. The definite quotient has discrete automorphic spectrum. A nonzero constituent of f has the same almost-everywhere split eigenvalues. Labesse’s Corollaire 5.3 applies because the compact real groups satisfy its sign condition and E contains Q(ζ₅₀₄₀), hence [E⁺:Q]≥2. It gives a weak base change to a sum of discrete GL blocks with the required cohomological infinitesimal character. Chenevier–Harris Theorem 3.2.3 applies directly only to a cohomological conjugate-self-dual cuspidal GL representation. For the possible residual blocks use Mœglin–Waldspurger’s description as strings of twists of cuspidal representations. For a rank-r member τ|det|ᵗ of such a string, τ|det|^(t+(r−n)/2) is regular algebraic because its archimedean parameters are the corresponding subset of the distinct rank-n parameters, shifted to the rank-r integral parity. Harris–Lan–Taylor–Thorne Theorem A then gives the Galois representation for the specified ℓ. Taking the sum gives the rank-n Tate normalization, as in the proof of Newton–Thorne Corollary 1.3. This use of Labesse and Theorem A requires no splitting hypothesis at ℓ. At a split unramified place let α be the normalized Satake parameters. The eigenvalue t_j of the coset of diag(ϖ·1_j,1) is q^{j(n−j)/2}e_j(α). Twisting by |det|^{(1−n)/2} gives geometric Frobenius roots q^{(n−1)/2}α, hence polynomial coefficients (−1)^j q^{j(j−1)/2}t_j, exactly heckePoly. Prime-norm w are split under StablyUnram. Semisimplicity in characteristic zero supplies the trace-pairing condition. The epsilon choice in BaseLevel then satisfies Attached.
sources: G. Chenevier and M. Harris, Construction of automorphic Galois representations, II, Theorem 3.2.3, cohomological conjugate-self-dual cuspidal GL representations
J.-P. Labesse, Changement de base CM et séries discrètes, §5.1, Corollaire 5.3 and the compact-infinity observation immediately preceding it
C. Mœglin and J.-L. Waldspurger, Le spectre résiduel de GL(n), introductory theorem, pp. 605–606, and §I.11
M. Harris, K.-W. Lan, R. Taylor and J. Thorne, On the rigid cohomology of certain Shimura varieties, Theorem A and Corollary 7.14, Tate-normalized compatibility at unramified primes
J. Newton and J. Thorne, Symmetric power functoriality for holomorphic modular forms, §1, Theorem 1.2, Corollary 1.3 and its proof, together with the conventions for recᵀ before §1

LFunction_one_sub_eq_zero.verdict: A zero-reflection corollary for arbitrary Dirichlet characters with an explicit gamma-factor exception.
LFunction_one_sub_eq_zero.comparison: For modulus N≠0, Re(s)≠0 and s≠1, a zero of L(s,χ) gives either a zero of Lean's totalized gamma factor at s or a zero of L(1−s,χ⁻¹). Pass to the primitive inducing character. The deleted finite Euler factors cannot vanish at the original s off Re(s)=0. Use the primitive completed functional equation, with the zeta equation in conductor one. Gamma poles have value zero in this Lean convention. Return to the imprimitive character by multiplying the reflected value by the missing factors. A trivial zero at a gamma pole need not reflect to a zero.
sources: Montgomery and Vaughan, Multiplicative Number Theory I, Chapter 10, Corollaries 10.3 and 10.9

Lift.TateTwist.smallPart_spec.verdict: The Artin–Schreier–Witt sequence explains Frobenius surjectivity. The complete small-ideal and continuity package is unlocated in Herr.
Lift.TateTwist.smallPart_spec.comparison: Let Γ lie over G_p with open image, m≥0, and ρ be a Z_p-representation with (ρ(h)−1)y∈p^mT near 1 for each y. Fix a W(C♭)-linear map L from the diagonal tensor of ρ to M=W(C♭)⊗Z/p^m(1). Here S is the image of W(𝔪♭)·(1⊗1). The header continues after its local definition of S. It gives p^m M=0, surjectivity of φ−1, (φ−1)d∈S implying d is a scalar modulo S, injectivity of the scalar copy modulo S, and for every v the estimate L(hv−v)∈S near 1. Illusie §2.7, (2.7.1), gives the exact Artin–Schreier–Witt sequence for truncated Witt vectors in the étale topology. On an algebraically closed tilt this yields the Frobenius assertion for m≥1, and m=0 is trivial. Herr §2, Theorem 2.1, computes continuous Galois cohomology from an étale (φ,Γ)-module complex. Neither passage gives the entire assertion for this S and arbitrary L. The remaining comparison must track the ideal and its scalars in the Witt-vector quotient, and the estimate used separately at PeriodRings/BdR.lean:37 and KisinModuleDefs.lean:114–124.
sources: L. Herr, Sur la cohomologie galoisienne des corps p-adiques, Bulletin de la Société Mathématique de France 126 (1998), §2, Théorème 2.1, p. 572
L. Illusie, Complexe de de Rham-Witt, Astérisque 63 (1979), §2.7, Artin–Schreier–Witt sequence (2.7.1)

Orbital.harish_chandra_degree_and_orbita.verdict: Harish–Chandra's character and degree formulas and the stable orbital identity are located. The exact Haar and coefficient comparison for the compact statement is open.
Orbital.harish_chandra_degree_and_orbita.comparison: For U(p,q), n=p+q≥1 and l=2λ regular of the specified parity, opposite-sign differences in λ are at least 500n³+10n⁵. The formal degree is defined as (∫|ψ_λ|²)⁻¹ for the explicit Flensted–Jensen coefficient, with the Cayley-chart Haar density divided by vol U(n). The theorem gives the product of all positive λ_i−λ_j divided by ∏_{i<n}i!, and for every diagonal x with distinct unit-modulus entries, a signed sum over all S_n conjugate points of the orbital integrals of deg·conj(ψ_λ). It equals p!q! times the conjugate compact U(n)-character. Harish–Chandra I, Theorem 3, constructs the regular-Cartan eigendistribution. II, Theorem 16, identifies the discrete series, character and formal degree in the author's normalization. Hochs–Wang, proof of Corollary 4.10, gives the orbital trace of the degree-scaled matrix coefficient of a unit K-finite vector, and §6 gives the transformation to the compact inner form. Repeating each S_n/(S_p×S_q) coset explains p!q!, and dim(G/K)/2=pq explains the sign. To get this exact conjunction, identify ψ_λ and its conjugation convention, pass from the semisimple group with finite centre to U(p,q), and match both authors' centralizer and group Haar choices to the compact Cayley density. Without that normalization the claimed numerical formal degree changes with Haar scale.
sources: Harish-Chandra, Discrete series for semisimple Lie groups I, Acta Mathematica 113 (1965), §18, Theorem 3, pp. 288–291
Harish-Chandra, Discrete series for semisimple Lie groups II, Acta Mathematica 116 (1966), §41, Theorem 16, pp. 96–100
P. Hochs and H. Wang, Orbital integrals and K-theory classes, Annals of K-Theory 4 (2019), proof of Corollary 4.10 and §§6A–6D, especially Theorem 6.4

ParamsCorrespond.isEdge_jointHarmonic.verdict: The formal matching condition selects witnesses for a two-sided analytic statement beyond the published joint-type criterion.
ParamsCorrespond.isEdge_jointHarmonic.comparison: The positive-rank and parameter-matching assumptions include large gaps and matching at every infinite place. The definition jointHarmonic chooses one polynomial per place by Hilbert choice. Given ParamsCorrespond, exists_isJointHarmonic makes each choice a genuine witness. Lean multiplies the polynomials in separate variables and applies isEdge_of_isJointHarmonic. The result includes the two nonzero real kernel integrals, level-conditional transfer of type, and compactly supported convolution expressions for lifts with all polynomial vectors. Ichino's Lemma 7.8 identifies irreducible compact types appearing together in the local joint-harmonic space. His Theorem 4.1 concerns the local theta lift of a discrete series. An analytic bridge to these particular integral projectors and their global lifting property remains open from those statements.
sources: Ichino, Theta lifting for discrete series representations of real unitary groups, Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 7.8, pp. 35–36 for the compact types
Pinned choice of local polynomials and proof of the edge for the chosen product

Place.plancherel_inequality.verdict: A one-sided consequence of abelian Plancherel with the compact normalization. Tate's local-field calculation accounts for the local-field case.
Place.plancherel_inequality.comparison: The domain A in General/Measure/Place.lean:18–38 is a locally compact Polish commutative ring with involution, additive Haar measure μ, unitary character ψ, modulus md, units of full measure, and an integrable nonnegative continuous G with G(0)=1 and ∫|∫G(v)ψ(v̄z)dμ(v)|dμ(z)≤c. For η a unit, finite ι and measurable f∈L¹(A^ι), Lean bounds the squared L² integral of its transform by (c/md(η))^|ι| times that of f, allowing infinity. Tate §§2.2.1–2.2.2 use a self-dual measure on a local field. For all such rings the relevant source is Cartan–Godement's abelian inversion and Plancherel. Here is the additional normalization argument. If c is finite, write Θ(z)(v)=ψ(v̄z). Since ∫G>0, continuity of the Fourier transform makes |Ĝ| bounded below on a dual neighbourhood W, so Θ⁻¹(W) has finite measure. For a closed neighbourhood W₀ with W₀W₀⊂W, its inverse image is compact. Indeed, for arbitrarily small open U with positive Haar measure and Θ(U)⊂W₀, only finitely many disjoint translates of U centred in Θ⁻¹(W₀) fit into Θ⁻¹(W). Thus Θ⁻¹(W₀) is closed and totally bounded. This gives closed image and compact kernel. The kernel is an ideal, and units tending to zero preserve that ideal. Their multiplication tends to zero uniformly on the compact ideal, which must therefore vanish. The annihilator of Θ(A) is the conjugate of that kernel, hence zero. Pontryagin duality now identifies A topologically with its full dual. If Θ_*μ=Cμ̂ for dual Haar μ̂, inversion at zero gives C≤C∫|Ĝ|dμ̂≤c. The involution preserves Haar because its positive modulus squares to one. Multiplication by η contributes md(η)⁻¹ in each coordinate. Product Plancherel gives equality at (C/md(η))^|ι|, implying the stated bound. Infinite c, f=0 almost everywhere, infinite right-hand integral and the zero-dimensional product give their immediate limiting cases.
sources: J. Tate, Fourier analysis in number fields and Hecke’s zeta-functions (1950), §2.2, Theorems 2.2.1–2.2.2, self-duality and self-dual additive Haar measure

H. Cartan and R. Godement, Théorie de la dualité et analyse harmonique dans les groupes abéliens localement compacts, Annales scientifiques de l’É.N.S. 64 (1947), §§IV–VI, inversion, Plancherel and duality

SUnit.dirichlet_unit_theorem.verdict: The algebraic finite-generation and rank assertions are exactly Dirichlet's S-unit theorem.
SUnit.dirichlet_unit_theorem.comparison: For an arbitrary number field K and a finite set S of its finite places, the additive copy of its S-unit group is a finitely generated ℤ-module with rank + 1 = |S| + |InfinitePlace(K)|. Neukirch includes all infinite places in his S. Taking his set to be the Lean S together with those infinite places gives rank |S|+r₁+r₂−1, with a conjugate pair counted once. His kernel consists of the finite group of roots of unity and his logarithmic image is a full lattice of the asserted rank. The Lean declaration states the abstract finite generation and integer rank. The proof at lines 91–111 uses the valuation map to ℤ^S, whose kernel is the ordinary units and whose image has finite index by finiteness of the class group.
sources: J. Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory (1999), VI §1, Proposition (1.1), pp. 358–359, including the proof by valuations at finite places. The ordinary-unit case is I §7, Theorem (7.4), p. 42.
Pinned S-unit valuation and rank argument, AdeleNorm.lean 91–111.

Space.IsForm.mem_rapidFunctions.verdict: Borel and Miller–Schmid establish rapid decay for cuspidal automorphic forms. A primary result starting from this full continuous convolution-kernel definition remains unlocated.
Space.IsForm.mem_rapidFunctions.comparison: Over a CM field with finite rank and sign pattern s, IsForm requires F continuous, left invariant under the rational unitary group, fixed by some open finite-adelic subgroup, bounded, and reproduced by R(e). An IsCuspKernel of order B is a continuous L¹ Hermitian minimal convolution idempotent with e(1)≠0, an integrable (B+1)-st operator-norm moment, bounded B-th weighted norm, and α*e=e for some continuous compactly supported α. The conclusion bounds |F(g)|·height(g)^A for every natural A, where height is the inverse clipped first minimum of the moved lattice. Borel’s Theorem 7.9 assumes cuspidality and trivial split central component and gives fast decrease on Siegel sets. Miller–Schmid Theorem A covers smooth cuspidal automorphic forms of moderate growth without right K-finiteness. Neither statement establishes the requisite smoothness and vanishing of the proper parabolic constant terms for every e in the compact definition, or identifies their Siegel-set norms with this height. The Lean proof instead uses oscillation along unipotent orbits, a uniform estimate relative to sup |F| for each fixed finite level, and arithmetic reduction of the height. The concrete discrete-series kernels supply examples of e. The quoted primary theorems do not cover the full class by inspection.
sources: A. Borel, Automorphic forms on reductive groups, §§7.6–7.9 and 8.1–8.4, pp. 20–24 of the lecture text
S. D. Miller and W. Schmid, On the rapid decay of cuspidal automorphic forms, Theorem A and Theorems 2.23–2.24
G. Muić, Smooth cuspidal automorphic forms and integrable discrete series, §6, Lemma 6-3 and Theorem 6-4, and §7, Theorem 7-6

Space.Splitting.iwasawa.verdict: Adelic Iwasawa decomposition for the parabolic preserving a prescribed isotropic flag, with the compact subgroup identified in coordinates.
Space.Splitting.iwasawa.comparison: Arthur §1, p. 917, fixes a compact subgroup satisfying the specialness and archimedean compatibility conditions and writes G(A)=P(A)K, then expands the parabolic factor into unipotent and Levi factors. In the present unitary group the weight function on the indices of a rational isotropic frame specifies a flag inside its span. Its stabilizer acts on this frame through matrices block upper triangular for that weight. Decomposing such a stabilizer element relative to the parabolic of the full span gives exactly the radical element and the Levi pair (b,u) in the conclusion. The source fixes its compact subgroup in advance, the standard compact at infinity times the finite integral group. Lines 67–81 verify the required flag transitivity with orthonormal frames at infinity and primitive integral frames at the finite adeles. First's Corollary 4.9 is an extension theorem for isometries and bears on this input.
sources: Arthur, A trace formula for reductive groups I, §1, p. 917, conditions (i)–(iii) and G(A)=P(A)K
First, Witt’s extension theorem for quadratic spaces over semiperfect rings, Corollary 4.9

Space.Splitting.zeroTerm.verdict: Choice of a proved bounded operator. The published mixed-model evaluation uses different spaces.
Space.Splitting.zeroTerm.comparison: For a fixed splitting D, the definition chooses the witness in exists_zeroTerm (535–552). That lemma constructs a continuous complex-linear map from the project's normed space of data on V to the corresponding space on V₀. Its value at y is the normalized mean of f(i y + k b) over the additive adelic quotient by rational b. zeroTerm_apply (560–561) gives this formula for the chosen witness, so pointwise equality determines the operator. The existence proof uses an adapted frame, a strong integral, uniqueness up to scalar of the invariant theta functional and an operator-norm bound. Gan–Qiu–Takeda define their Ikeda map on adelic Schwartz–Bruhat functions by integrating on a full adelic linear space, equivalently evaluating a partial Fourier transform at zero. Identifying their data space, measures and evaluation with this bounded quotient-mean operator requires a model comparison.
sources: Gan, Qiu and Takeda, The regularized Siegel–Weil formula, §2.7, definition of the Ikeda map and the partial Fourier transform diagram, p. 12 of the preprint

Space.exists_eq_move.verdict: Landherr's local–global equivalence, expressed in the coordinates of two framed spaces.
Space.exists_eq_move.comparison: The spaces have the same real signature data, and their adelic frames give local isometries at every finite place. Landherr supplies a rational isometry a with a*J_V a=J_W. In these coordinates set g by g=V.x⁻¹·a·W.x in the appropriate unitary factors. The Gram identities put g in the required group. Rearrangement gives the stated frame equality, and conjugating an arbitrary rational γ gives the equality of the two embeddings. The equality for every γ is an additional coordinate identity, available once the rational isometry has been chosen.
sources: Landherr, Äquivalenz Hermitescher Formen über einem beliebigen algebraischen Zahlkörper, pp. 246–247, especially the local–global equivalence on p. 247

Space.exists_kernel_form.verdict: Godement’s holomorphic Poincaré series and Muić’s discrete-series constructions have extra hypotheses. Muić’s compact-support argument explains the project’s pointwise periodization.
Space.exists_kernel_form.comparison: Fix any translate x and an open subgroup K contained in the standard compact K₀ at the finite places. For the continuous cusp kernel e and the rational subgroup Γ, a bounded continuous K-fixed form k reproduced by e satisfies conjugate(k(g))=Σγ e((xγg)∞)1_K((xγg)f) at every g. The assertion allows k=0. Godement’s Théorème 5 works on the Siegel domain for holomorphic H¹ sections, and 5 bis assumes a K-finiteness condition and the bound on lowest weight. Muić’s Theorems 6-4 and 7-6 concern integrable discrete series with a specified K-finite vector and smooth cuspidal vectors. Neither theorem identifies every continuous kernel here. Muić’s Lemma 6-3 provides an argument that adapts directly. Write e=α*e with α continuous and compactly supported. A translate of the compact support of α⊗1_K meets a Γ-coset in uniformly boundedly many points, by finiteness of Γ intersected with the product of the support and its inverse. Periodize the translate of conjugate(α)⊗1_K, then convolve at infinity with e. The uniform multiplicity bound and ‖e‖₁ justify interchange, give a bounded continuous sum, and e*e=e gives reproduction. The Hermitian involution yields the conjugation in the formula. The cited quantifiers for smooth or holomorphic input still differ from the pinned theorem.
sources: R. Godement, Série de Poincaré et Spitzenformen, Séminaire Henri Cartan 10, Exposé 10, §4, Théorèmes 5 and 5 bis
G. Muić, Smooth cuspidal automorphic forms and integrable discrete series, §6, Lemma 6-3 and Theorem 6-4, and §7, Theorem 7-6

Space.exists_mapsTo_ratVectors.verdict: Landherr's local-to-global isometry for two adelically framed hermitian spaces.
Space.exists_mapsTo_ratVectors.comparison: Landherr proves that nondegenerate hermitian forms over a quadratic extension of number fields are equivalent when they are equivalent at every completion. Here both spaces carry adelic frames for the same standard form. These give all local isometries, including the finite ones. Space.landherr supplies a rational change of basis, and exists_eq_move (Landherr.lean 91–96) conjugates it by the two adelic frames. The resulting element of the standard adelic unitary group carries each rational vector of V into the rational vectors of W in the chosen coordinates. The one-way inclusion and the hypotheses supplied by the frames are exactly what the declaration uses.
sources: Landherr, Äquivalenz Hermitescher Formen über einem beliebigen algebraischen Zahlkörper, pp. 246–247, classification by invariants and the local-global statement on p. 247
Landherr, Äquivalenz Hermitescher Formen über einem beliebigen algebraischen Zahlkörper, original journal article, volume 11, pp. 245–248

Space.exists_short_basis.verdict: Banaszczyk’s Euclidean transference bound plus the trace-dual calculation gives a smaller radius for an E-basis of lattice vectors.
Space.exists_short_basis.comparison: Let E be CM, f its number of infinite places, n its finite rank, N a nonzero natural number in the different, and L the image of V.baseLattice in the Euclidean space of real dimension m=2fn via archCoords. The signs of the Hermitian form may vary. Set λ=min(1,λ₁(L)). The statement produces an E-basis inside L of length at most 6N(fn)²/λ. The columns may generate a proper sublattice. MassBasic.lean:29–64 identifies each nonzero member of the real Euclidean dual of (2/N)L with a vector of the same length in L, using the trace pairing, the finite Hermitian self-duality condition, and N in the different. Thus λ₁(((2/N)L)*)≥λ. Banaszczyk (2.1), i=m, gives λ_m((2/N)L)≤m/λ. Scaling back, L contains m real-linearly independent vectors of length at most Nm/(2λ)=Nfn/λ. They span the real Minkowski space. Their E-span is Eⁿ because an E-subspace of rank k<n has a real Minkowski span of dimension 2fk. Select n E-independent vectors. For fn≥1 this radius implies the larger stated radius, and the rank-zero case uses the empty basis. The Lean argument uses a weaker covering-radius estimate and an induction. Lagarias–Lenstra–Schnorr Theorems 2.4–2.5 give the earlier reciprocal-minima and covering-radius inequalities.
sources: W. Banaszczyk, New bounds in some transference theorems in the geometry of numbers, Math. Ann. 296 (1993), Theorems (2.1) and (2.2), pp. 631–632
J. C. Lagarias, H. W. Lenstra Jr. and C. P. Schnorr, Korkin-Zolotarev bases and successive minima of a lattice and its reciprocal lattice, Theorems 2.4–2.5, pp. 336–337

Space.exists_splitting.verdict: Combination of hermitian local-global classification and Witt extension with a fixed isotropic frame.
Space.exists_splitting.comparison: The output fixes the given rational frame k exactly. It supplies a dual isotropic frame l with l*Jk=1, an orthogonal inclusion of the complement, the rank equality, and a Space on the complement. Space includes an adelic frame with the specified signs at infinity and identity Gram matrix at finite places. Witness the complement by the signed model obtained after deleting one positive and one negative direction per isotropic column. The rank bounds in the proof permit these deletions. The ambient framed space and this hyperbolic sum are everywhere locally isometric, so Landherr supplies a rational isometry. Witt extension transports its isotropic frame to the prescribed k. First, Remark 2.1 and Corollary 4.9, apply to hermitian forms over the characteristic-zero field. Witt's original Satz 5 splits off a hyperbolic plane for quadratic forms. The claimed pointed hermitian statement uses both the classification and the frame extension.
sources: Landherr, Äquivalenz Hermitescher Formen über einem beliebigen algebraischen Zahlkörper, p. 247, equivalence at all completions
First, Witt’s extension theorem for quadratic spaces over semiperfect rings, Remark 2.1 and Corollary 4.9
Witt, Theorie der quadratischen Formen in beliebigen Körpern, Satz 5

Space.exists_trace_eq.verdict: Labesse and Arthur–Clozel supply trace-formula inputs with different test functions and transfer statements
Space.exists_trace_eq.comparison: Let E be a CM field with a primitive 5040th root of unity and an even number of infinite places, n a nonempty finite rank. Let K be a level in the finite adelic unitary group, h an element such that every point of hK has irreducible characteristic polynomial at some finite place (which can depend on the point). Require B≥16[E:ℚ](|n|+1)^3, H≥500|n|^3+10|n|^5. For given l,H there is one scalar t for every signature, hermitian space V and orthonormal basis of its K-level type-kernel space, whenever the type kernel is cuspidal of order B and all Harish–Chandra parameters have gap H. Then Σ_i⟨b_i,h·b_i⟩=t. Labesse 5.1 compares stabilized distributions and 5.4 proves weak cuspidal base change/multiplicity one under hypotheses on finite inert places; its proof compares stable orbital integrals using pseudo-coefficients, with measure and sign normalizations. Arthur–Clozel I.2.4–2.6 give ordinary/twisted GL simple trace formulas and compactness under particular local test functions. Neither citation gives this fixed finite coset and the explicit rapid-decay/gap conditions or the scalar equality simultaneously for all these unitary spaces. The project's packing estimates and comparison of archimedean orbital terms furnish the extra argument.
sources: J.-P. Labesse, Changement de base CM et séries discrètes, Théorème 5.1 (trace identity, p. 41) and §5.2, Théorème 5.4 with proof (pp. 45–46 of author copy). The latter gives cuspidal weak base change and conditional multiplicity one.

J. Arthur and L. Clozel, Simple Algebras, Base Change, and the Advanced Theory of the Trace Formula, I §2, Lemmas 2.4–2.6, pp. 13–15. Ordinary and twisted simple trace formulas and compactness of a kernel under the stated supercuspidal/regular elliptic test-function conditions.
The ambient bounds and the quantification of a single trace over signatures and spaces.

Space.finite_levelSpace.verdict: Godement’s finite-dimensionality lemma in Borel §8.3 applies after the project’s uniform height bound and compactness criterion. Harish-Chandra’s fixed-type theorem in §8.4 has different hypotheses.
Space.finite_levelSpace.comparison: For any open subgroup K of the finite adelic unitary group, the bounded continuous rationally invariant forms fixed by K and reproduced by e form a finite-dimensional complex space. The full IsCuspKernel hypotheses are those at RealConvolution.lean:74–77, and K may contain a smaller compact open subgroup K′. Borel §8.4 fixes a finite-codimensional ideal of the center of the enveloping algebra and a standard idempotent for a maximal compact group. The Lean assumptions specify neither. There is an independent route from §8.3. The project proves finite quotient volume and, for fixed K′ and e, |F(g)|·height(g)≤R‖F‖∞.
