Mahler compactness puts a representative of every coset with height at most 2R in one compact set C, and outside this set modulo rational translates |F|≤‖F‖∞/2. On C, F=R(α)F for the compactly supported continuous α satisfying α*e=e. Averaging also over K′, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds |F| by a constant times its quotient L² norm, since the support swept out by C, supp α and K′ is compact and its rational translates have uniformly finite overlap. Thus ‖F‖∞≤C′‖F‖₂. An L²-Cauchy sequence of such forms converges uniformly to a continuous bounded rationally invariant function of level K′, and the L¹ convolution reproduces the limit. The subspace is closed in the finite-measure quotient L² and consists of bounded functions, which are precisely Godement’s hypotheses. Passing to the K-fixed subspace gives the claimed result.
sources: A. Borel, Automorphic forms on reductive groups, §§7.6–7.9 and 8.1–8.4, pp. 20–24 of the lecture text

Space.weak_approximation.verdict: Weak approximation on a rational unitary group, with unconstrained finite components represented by a subgroup.
Space.weak_approximation.comparison: For a Hermitian CM space the unitary group over the real subfield is smooth, connected and rational: the Cayley transform identifies dense opens of the skew-adjoint endomorphisms and the unitary group in characteristic zero. Proposition 7.3 therefore gives simultaneous approximation at all infinite places and a prescribed finite set. Matching the remaining components by an element of the subgroup trivial on that set gives the dense-range expression used in Lean. At split pairs use the conjugation-stable closure of the set. The formal proof constructs the approximation by a Cayley map. There is no requirement of integrality at every uncontrolled place for the rational element.
sources: Platonov and Rapinchuk, Algebraic Groups and Number Theory, Chapter 7, §7.1, Proposition 7.3, weak approximation for smooth rational varieties

Space.witt.verdict: The field-level extension theorem evaluated on the Hermitian matrix of the supplied CM space.
Space.witt.comparison: The two left-invertible coordinate matrices with equal restricted Gram matrices define an isometry on their images. The CM involution supplies a z distinct from its conjugate, and the definition of the space supplies a Hermitian, invertible J. The field theorem then extends the map of columns to g in U(J)(E). No adelic approximation or integral extension is required in this declaration.
sources: First, Witt's extension theorem for quadratic spaces over semiperfect rings, Corollary 4.9

SplitPlaces.hasFewCocycles_of_central.verdict: The Greenberg–Wiles formula compares two Selmer groups in H¹. A published derivation of this absolute count of trivialised cocycles was not located.
SplitPlaces.hasFewCocycles_of_central.comparison: K is totally complex, ℓ prime, r and N positive, and an open normal U with a finite family of auxiliary primes satisfies SplitPlaces for m=ℓ^r. This includes m|N, U fixing μ_m and containing inertia off N, pairwise distinct vᵢ away from N with chosen Frobenii φᵢ in U, the prescribed inertia set I away from N and the vᵢ, and generation by the primes above N of class groups of the intermediate fields inside Ω^U. V is a finite discrete module over a commutative ring, killed by m and U-fixed. The element z is central modulo U, has ℓ-adic cyclotomic character 1, and ρ(z)−1 is injective on V. Every m-th root of an N-unit in Ω^U fixed by all φᵢ must be fixed by U. Lean bounds the number of pairs (f,c), where f is V-valued on places over N and infinity, c is continuous and zero on I, and ρ(g)f(x)=f(gx)+c(g). The order is positive and at most |V|^(|ι|+1). Darmon–Diamond–Taylor 2.19 gives a ratio of orders of two Selmer subgroups of H¹ over a number field, in terms of local conditions and H⁰. Identifying the absolute count here needs the local conditions, the numbers of trivializations and coboundaries, and control of the dual contribution via the given root-detection and centrality hypotheses. The published ratio alone does not perform these steps.
sources: H. Darmon, F. Diamond and R. Taylor, Fermat's Last Theorem, author text dated 24 May 2000, §2.3, Theorem 2.18 for ℚ, p. 61, and Theorem 2.19 for any number field, p. 62.
A. Wiles, Modular elliptic curves and Fermat's Last Theorem, Annals of Mathematics 141 (1995), §1.2, Proposition 1.6, pp. 472–473, gives the ratio for odd-primary modules over ℚ.
J. S. Milne, Arithmetic Duality Theorems, 2nd ed., I §4, Theorem 4.10, pp. 56–57, and I §5, Theorem 5.1 (global Euler characteristic). These are cohomological inputs to the ratio.
Pinned definitions of the auxiliary primes, I and Frobenius detection, SelmerBasic.lean 91–123.
Pinned pair space and Nat.card bound, DiscreteUnits.lean 157–165.

amitsur_charpoly_mem_of_span.verdict: Coefficient descent on a spanning family follows from the integral Amitsur formula.
amitsur_charpoly_mem_of_span.comparison: For a representation of a B-algebra in matrices over a commutative B-algebra A, the good elements have all characteristic coefficients in the image of B. Assume they span the source over B. Amitsur's formula for a finite sum involves coefficients of products of summands. In characteristic degree j, a word of length at least two occurs with coefficient index strictly below j. Induction in j therefore applies to that product as another element of the algebra. The length-one terms come from the spanning family, with the scalar powers in the image of B. This gives descent without injectivity of the base map, denominators or a characteristic-zero assumption. The Lean conclusion gives no formula for the coefficients.
sources: Chenevier, The p-adic analytic space of pseudocharacters of a profinite group and pseudorepresentations over arbitrary rings, §1, equation (1.5), Amitsur's formula

artinMap_surjective.verdict: surjectivity from finite idèles follows from global reciprocity and weak approximation
artinMap_surjective.comparison: For a number field K with a pro-Galois realization Γ of its absolute Galois group, Lean proves that the project's finite-idèle Artin homomorphism is onto the topological abelianization. Milne states surjectivity on the full idèle class group and identifies its kernel. To obtain finite-idèle representatives in the image, match the signs at the real places by an element of K×, using weak approximation. After division the infinite component is in the connected identity component, whose image in the profinite group is trivial. Principal idèles also map trivially for the full map. The project's convention is fixed by its local maps on finite components. Inverting the Frobenius normalization would preserve surjectivity. Lean's statement makes no assertion about the kernel.
sources: Milne, Class Field Theory, v4.03, Introduction pp. 11–12, global idèle-class reciprocity
Pinned definition of the finite-idèle homomorphism in terms of the local Artin maps, lines 99–108

avatarCompatAt_of_stablyUnram.verdict: Rank-one local character theory with CM and root-of-unity restrictions, a convention change, and two Weil degrees
avatarCompatAt_of_stablyUnram.comparison: For a finite place w of an embedded CM field E containing a primitive 5040th root and any algebraic Hecke character θ, use its already-defined scalar ℓ-adic avatar. At every A above w it has finite type, and at embeddings above ℓ the jumps are minus the transported infinity weights with multiplicity one. For m=0 or 1 and any s with s⁻¹ acting on residues by (Nw)^m, it supplies x with ordinary order +m (v(x)=exp(−m)) and geometric Artin image [s]. The polynomial X−ιθ_w(x) kills s in the project's sense. Away from ℓ this is scalar evaluation on r(s); at ℓ it is evaluation on the associated period Frobenius. Serre's local algebraicity/Hodge–Tate criterion applies to abelian semisimple characters. Conrad B.3 computes labelled weights and B.4 gives crystallinity for a character algebraic on the entire unit group, together with a crystalline Frobenius formula. Potential crystallinity of a locally algebraic character follows after a finite extension eliminating its finite unit factor. One must use the inverse of Conrad's arithmetic reciprocity and translate Hodge–Tate conventions, compare the local factor with the global avatar, and use local reciprocity for x. The compact proof obtains the result via its rank-one spherical case and quadratic descent.
sources: J.-P. Serre, Abelian ℓ-adic Representations and Elliptic Curves, III §1.2, pp. III-5–III-7, theorem on p. III-7: local algebraicity is equivalent to Hodge–Tate type together with semisimplicity on inertia for abelian representations.

B. Conrad, Lifting global representations with local properties, Appendix B, Definition B.1, p. 32, Proposition B.3, p. 33, and Proposition B.4(i)–(ii), p. 35 of the author text. The Artin map in that appendix has arithmetic normalization.

J.-P. Serre, Local Fields, XIV §2, Proposition 6, p. 208, and §3, Proposition 8 and finite-field corollary, pp. 210–211. The Kummer ratio computes the prime-to-p norm residue symbol, with arithmetic reciprocity.
Pinned predicate AvatarCompatAt and the Frobenius convention.
Pinned definitions of good type, finite type, jumps and PolyKillsAt in the two residue-characteristic cases.

cartan_decomposition.verdict: An explicit rank-one double-coset decomposition with the phase fixed, obtained by unitary transitivity on vectors of equal length.
cartan_decomposition.comparison: The last floor acts on X₀⊕ℂz with X₀ positive definite and z of negative norm. For σ in this floor with last frame entry c satisfying |c|>1, the factors on both sides of cellChart(c) lie in U(X₀) and fix z itself. Knapp's KAK theorem uses a full maximal compact and specifies a radial parameter up to the Weyl group. Here the complex phase of c also labels a double coset, because the stabilizer is smaller. Write the column of the moved z in its X₀ and z components. Preserving the Hermitian norm gives length √(|c|²−1) for its X₀ component. The model boost at ComplexPlace.lean:79–87 has precisely that length and the specified last entry. Theorem 3.4 of Sprehn–Wahl extends the isometry of the two equal-length complex lines to U(X₀). After that left multiplication the columns agree, so the remaining quotient fixes z and lies in U(X₀), giving the right factor. This proves the extra phase and stabilizer assertions in the given range.
sources: A. Knapp, Structure theory of semisimple Lie groups, Theorem 4.10, KAK decomposition
D. Sprehn and N. Wahl, Forms over fields and Witt's lemma, Theorem 3.4, extension of subspace isometries

chebotarev.verdict: existence consequence of finite Galois Chebotarev, with a chosen place above the prime
chebotarev.comparison: Given a nonempty open W in the absolute Galois group and a finite set of excluded places, Lean produces a place of prime norm outside that set and a place above it admitting a Frobenius lift in W, with every such lift at that place in W. Choose a coset gU inside W for an open normal subgroup U. Finite Galois Chebotarev supplies a positive-density set with Frobenius conjugate to g in the quotient. Exclude the prescribed places and the degree-greater-than-one places, which have Dirichlet density zero. Conjugating the choice of the place above the prime realizes the specified representative. Inertia acts trivially in the unramified finite quotient, so every Frobenius lift at that chosen place maps to that representative. The conclusion uses no quantitative density.
sources: Milne, Class Field Theory, v4.03, Chapter VIII §7, Theorem 7.4

classAut_eq_bot.verdict: A quantitative trace-norm neatness lemma for CM ideal levels, requiring an additional argument beyond integral integer level
classAut_eq_bot.comparison: Let E have a CM type and at least two infinite places. Let w_i be a finite injective family of finite places and let (2|n|)^[E:ℚ] < ∏_i Nw_i. For any K contained in the principal congruence level there and every finite adelic translate g, the intersection of the rational definite-unitary group with the conjugate level is trivial. Serre's appendix treats finite-order automorphisms of abelian varieties acting trivially modulo an integer N≥3, by a root-of-unity argument in their endomorphism algebra. A product of distinct prime ideals of large norm need not impose that integer-level congruence, and the groups are different. The Lean proof puts tr(γ−1) in the congruence ideal, bounds its absolute norm using unit-modulus roots at the complex places, and forces it to vanish. Positivity of the definite form then forces γ=1. The catalogue note's claim that it bounds all characteristic-polynomial coefficients does not describe these lines.
sources: J.-P. Serre, Rigidité du foncteur de Jacobi d'échelon n ≥ 3, appendix to A. Grothendieck, Séminaire Cartan 13 (1960–61), exposé 17, pp. 17-18–17-20, theorem at p. 17-19. The input is a finite-order automorphism of an abelian variety congruent to 1 modulo an integer.
The trace, norm divisibility and final positive-definite argument in the pinned proof.

classSum_norm_eq.verdict: Weil's mean-value identity on a nonzero index fiber, with the one-vector constants worked out in the formal source.
classSum_norm_eq.comparison: Weil, §52, Theorem 5, equation (41), equates the probability-normalized mean of the rational representation sum at a specified index with the gauge-measure integral on that fiber. The unitary case has ε=1/2, so his convergence bound m>2n+4ε−2 gives m≥3 for one vector. Lean chooses the standard definite sum of m norms, a totally positive self-conjugate index, an open subgroup of the finite integral unitary group, and a nonnegative, locally constant, compactly supported level-invariant finite test function. The formal proof converts the normalized group average into the class sum multiplied by its total mass (lines 128–135). It uses its codifferent and Haar conventions to obtain |disc E|^{1/4} (111–123), and the real Gaussian/Fourier integrals give π^m α_v^{m−1}/(m−1)! at each infinite place (136–141). The remaining density is the finite adelic Fourier integral with the explicit factor 1/2 in its character. Equation (41) supplies the invariant mean identity. These displayed constants come from the coordinate computation in Lean.
sources: Weil, Sur la formule de Siegel dans la théorie des groupes classiques, §52, Theorem 5, equation (41), pp. 76–77, referring to §44 for the gauge
Pinned conversion of measures, finite class sum and archimedean integral

crysCocycles.apply_eq_zero_of_cyclotomic.verdict: Evaluation vanishing follows from the calculation of the finite local condition for twists.
crysCocycles.apply_eq_zero_of_cyclotomic.comparison: T is finite free over Z_p with action ρ(g)=χ(j(g))^(−a) for a natural number a. The image j(Γ)=G_K is open. For any integral c satisfying the B_max-coboundary equation for all g, and s with ρ(s)=1, Lean proves c(s)=0, assuming also j(s)∈I_K when a=0. The action already factors through j and its period equation forces c to descend. Tate twists are crystalline and CocycleContinuity.lean:70–72 gives continuity of the descended cocycle. Tensoring with Q_p gives a direct sum of Q_p(−a). Colmez III.4 identifies B_max and B_cris invariants for the finite-dimensional extension defined by c, so the extension has a fixed lift of 1 for either period ring. Bloch–Kato Example 3.9 gives H¹_f(K,Q_p(r))=0 for r<0, so c is a rational coboundary and vanishes wherever ρ(s)=1. For a=0 it gives unramified classes, so the cocycle for the trivial representation vanishes on inertia. In both cases the injection T→T[1/p] gives the integral assertion.
sources: S. Bloch and K. Kato, L-functions and Tamagawa numbers of motives, The Grothendieck Festschrift I (1990), §3.7 and Example 3.9, p. 359
P. Colmez, Théorie d’Iwasawa des représentations de de Rham d’un corps local, §III.4, D_cris and Tate twists

crysCocycles.finrank_eq.verdict: The Bloch–Kato local dimension formula applied to the integral module of actual cocycles.
crysCocycles.finrank_eq.comparison: Let T be finite free over Z_p with an action of Γ linear over a compatible commutative Z_p-algebra R, with j(Γ)=G_K open in G_p. Assume potential crystallinity and that J gives the Hodge–Tate jumps on restriction of scalars to Z_p. The B_max-coboundary condition of Defs.lean:51–56 cuts out Z_f(T) among maps Γ→T. Lean gives finite generation over Z_p and rank rank(T)+[K:Q_p]·#(u∈J with u<0), with multiplicity. Every kernel element of j fixes the spanning periods. It acts trivially on B_max⊗T and hence on T. The coboundary equation also forces c to descend to G_K. CocycleContinuity.lean:70–72 gives continuity modulo each p^n for c. Applying it to integral coboundaries on a basis gives continuity of the descended representation. On V=T[1/p], a rational cocycle satisfies the B_max condition exactly when its extension of Q_p by V admits an invariant lift of 1 over B_max. Colmez III.4 identifies these invariant spaces with those over B_cris, including for the extension. Thus this is the Bloch–Kato finite local condition. Corollary 3.8.4 gives dim H¹_f=dim(D_dR/Fil⁰)+dim H⁰. Adding the coboundary dimension dim V−dim H⁰ gives the cocycle dimension. Fontaine III §3.8(i) and the filtered frame in CocycleContinuity.lean:18–23 give dim_Qp(D_dR/Fil⁰)=[K:Q_p]·#(u<0) in this jump convention. Compactness scales every continuous rational cocycle into T. Finitely many coordinate evaluations separate the finite-dimensional rational space and embed Z_f(T) into a finite power of Z_p, giving finite generation. These steps account for the integral, open-image and cocycle formulations.
sources: S. Bloch and K. Kato, L-functions and Tamagawa numbers of motives, The Grothendieck Festschrift I (1990), §3.7.2–3 and Corollary 3.8.4, pp. 353–355
P. Colmez, Théorie d’Iwasawa des représentations de de Rham d’un corps local, §§III.2 and III.4, equality of crystalline period spaces
J.-M. Fontaine, Représentations p-adiques semi-stables, Exposé III, Theorem 3.8(i), graded de Rham comparison

dsCoeff_eq_holMinors.verdict: The published holomorphic-chamber criterion is located. The equality of the two explicit normalized functions remains unlocated.
dsCoeff_eq_holMinors.comparison: Here n is finite and nonempty. Choose an injective order o with positive signs first, a K-dominant integral weight w, and natural A and γ with w_i+γ≤w_j for each positive i and negative j, and γ>500n³+A+n+1. For l=2w+twoRho(−o) the full conclusion, beyond the local let in the census range, is HasLargeGap A and pointwise ψ_l(g)=holMinors ε w g on U(diag ε). This is a single group. The left side is the normalized compact integral in RepresentationDefs.lean:103–115. The right side is its particular quotient of products of principal minors at lines 176–181. Korányi recovers Harish–Chandra's holomorphic-discrete-series condition and determines the holomorphic kernel from its multiplier. In the relevant chamber this supplies the holomorphic representation. The weight and gap normalization for l, the identification of the Flensted–Jensen integral with the evaluation coefficient of that representation and the exact scalar and minors formula still need a published comparison. The source uses a Casimir argument for holomorphicity and its own characterization by the value at 1.
sources: A. Korányi, A simplified approach to the holomorphic discrete series, §§3–4 on the representation and kernel, and §6, (6.4) and the comparison with Harish–Chandra's condition

Harish-Chandra, Representations of semisimple Lie groups V, American Journal of Mathematics 78 (1956), §§4–5 and §9 on holomorphic function spaces and unitarity. The exact compact minors identity remains unlocated.

dvd_differentIdeal_of_mem_sq.verdict: A divisibility consequence of the lower bound on the exponent of the different at a prime.
dvd_differentIdeal_of_mem_sq.comparison: The ideal P in the ring of integers is arbitrary. If a rational prime p belongs to P² then each prime ideal of exponent a>0 in P lies above p with ramification index e≥2a. The different exponent is at least e−1, hence at least a. Multiplying the prime powers proves P divides the different. The theorem asks for neither equality in the tame case nor a formula for the full different.
sources: Keith Conrad, The different ideal, Theorem 4.13 and its proof

ellAdicCohom.transfer.verdict: related descent formalism located; comparison with this cover remains open
ellAdicCohom.transfer.comparison: For two proper objects and a finite-group cover, pullback on rational ℓ-adic cohomology is injective and its image contains the invariant classes. The project's cover means a group action over the map, surjectivity and a simply transitive action on each nonempty fibre of characteristic-zero field-valued points. The definition is in LocalTerms.lean, lines 99–103. Grothendieck's Chapter V develops sheaves with group action and the case of a discontinuous group of homeomorphisms. A comparison with this specific algebraic cover and the project's cohomology functor still needs a proof or a separate reference. The Lean proof constructs a transfer and averages by the order of the group.
sources: Grothendieck, Sur quelques points d'algèbre homologique, Chapter V, §§5.2–5.3

entireL_ne_zero.verdict: direct consequence of two pinned Mathlib results after splitting the principal case
entireL_ne_zero.comparison: For every nonzero natural modulus N, every complex Dirichlet character χ modulo N, and every complex s with Re s ≥ 1, the project’s entireL χ s is nonzero. For nonprincipal χ, entireL is the ordinary L-function and Mathlib supplies the conclusion even at s = 1. For principal χ and s ≠ 1, it is (s−1)L(s,χ), whose two factors are nonzero. At the remaining point the definition assigns the finite product ∏_{p|N}(1−1/p) over distinct prime divisors, and Mathlib proves this value nonzero, including the empty product for N = 1. The compact proof invokes both cited declarations after unfolding entireL. No primitivity assumption occurs.
sources: Same revision, DirichletCharacter.LFunctionTrivChar₁ and LFunctionTrivChar₁_apply_one_ne_zero, DirichletContinuation.lean, lines 332–344.
Compact definition of entireL, QuadField.lean, lines 29–31.

exists_auerbach.verdict: A determinant-maximization extension of Auerbach's lemma with a prescribed compact separating family.
exists_auerbach.comparison: The given forms belong to the algebraic dual over a field K embedded in a normed field L. Their evaluations vary continuously in a compact parameter. The conclusion chooses coordinates from these very forms and gives the bound for every form in the family. The familiar real or complex normed-space theorem gives a biorthogonal unit basis but does not assert this selection from a given family in these fields. Maximizing a nonzero determinant over tuples of the family proves the extension using a one-row replacement. I have not located that precise version in a published source.
sources: Schlumprecht, Course notes for Functional Analysis I, Theorem 1.5.1, the classical unit-basis statement and proof

exists_comp_artinMap.verdict: The finite-idèle factorization for a totally complex number field follows from the kernel description in global reciprocity.
exists_comp_artinMap.comparison: Let K be totally complex and let Γ realize the full pro-Galois action on the closure Ω. The target C is a group with a T₁ topology. Even continuity of its group operations is absent from the hypotheses. The given homomorphism θ from the finite idèles is continuous and kills principal finite idèles. Lean produces a continuous group homomorphism μ from Γ satisfying μ(g)=θ(x) whenever Art(x) is the abelianized class of g. Milne V.5.7(a) identifies the kernel on full idèles as the closure of the product of the principal idèles with the connected factors at infinity. Here every infinite factor is connected, so Art on the finite idèles is onto, with kernel the closure of the principal finite idèles. The kernel of θ is closed by continuity and the T₁ hypothesis. Thus θ factors through the quotient, continuously by the quotient-map property, and pulling back along Γ to its abelianization supplies μ. The Lean statement selects a factor, with no separate family of norm compatibilities among its premises.
sources: J. S. Milne, Class Field Theory, v4.03, V §5, Reciprocity Theorem 5.3 and Existence Theorem 5.5, pp. 178–179, and Remark 5.7(a), pp. 179–180 (surjectivity and the closed kernel).
Pinned finite-idèle factorization, including the T₁ assumption and quotient-map proof, Avatars.lean 157–172.

exists_divStar.verdict: The quadratic finite-idèle component of idelic Hilbert 90
exists_divStar.comparison: For each norm-one adèle u of E, with conjugation over its maximal totally real subfield, Lean produces one invertible finite adèle y with finite-part identity u_f=y/ȳ. The archimedean part of u is unconstrained by the conclusion. Serre proves field Hilbert 90. Separate choices of arbitrary local solutions require a restricted-product argument to give an idèle: at almost all unramified nonsplit places the norm-one component is a unit and a solution can be scaled by a base-field uniformizer to become a unit. At split pairs one may put a component on one factor and 1 on the other. Milne proves H¹(G,I_E)=0 for the full idèles, including unit cohomology outside finitely many places. Apply it to the order-two conjugation and project a solution to the finite factors. This directly accounts for the restricted product in the Lean statement.
sources: J.-P. Serre, Local Fields, X §1, Proposition 2, p. 150, and cyclic corollary, p. 151. The coefficient group here is a field's multiplicative group.
J. S. Milne, Class Field Theory, VII §2, Proposition 2.5 and Corollary 2.6(a), pp. 205–206. The idèle cohomology decomposes into local groups, including the unramified integral-unit argument.
Compact finite-idèle form invoked in CharacterLevels.lean, IdeleHilbert90.lean, line 166 onward.

exists_entireL_quadTwist_ne_zero.verdict: real-character density theorem with an additional estimate needed for simultaneous complex twists
exists_entireL_quadTwist_ne_zero.comparison: Fix a nonzero natural modulus N, a real β > 1/2, any real y, and a unit a modulo N. Assume every prime d representing a is 7 modulo 8 and coprime to N. Lean produces a single prime d representing a such that, simultaneously for every complex Dirichlet character ξ modulo N and every complex s with Re s ≥ β and |Im s| ≤ y, the pole-removed L-function of ξ times the Legendre character modulo d is nonzero. When y is negative the zero condition is empty, but the theorem still produces a prime. Jutila’s Theorem 2 bounds the number of zeros in α ≤ Re s ≤ 1, |Im s| ≤ T, summed over real discriminant characters. For fixed T and 1/2 < α < 1 its exponent of X is strictly below one if ε is small enough. It controls exceptional real characters in a prime subfamily. For a nonreal ξ the product character is generally nonreal. Theorem 1 permits complex coefficients, but extending the zero detector to each fixed twist, handling imprimitive Euler factors, and taking the union over all characters modulo N are additional steps. The compact proof supplies its own per-character power-saving estimate in zero_density_quadTwist, then uses divergence of reciprocal primes in the reduced residue class. The cited Theorem 2 alone does not establish the full Lean statement. The catalogue should retain arbitrary y.
sources: M. Jutila, On mean values of Dirichlet polynomials with real characters, Acta Arith. 27 (1975), pp. 191–198. See the character family and Theorem 1 on p. 192 and Theorem 2, equation (6), on p. 193.
Compact proof, zero_density_quadTwist and exists_entireL_quadTwist_ne_zero, ZeroFreeTwist.lean, lines 147–206.

exists_eq_smul_haar.verdict: The full s-finite assertion extends regular Haar uniqueness and includes an infinite multiplier. There is a direct derivation from s-finite Tonelli.
exists_eq_smul_haar.comparison: On a second-countable locally compact Hausdorff group G, fix a left Haar measure μ also invariant on the right. Every s-finite right-invariant Borel measure ν satisfies ν=dμ for d∈[0,∞]. The zero measure and ∞·μ are both allowed. For comparison, van Doorn §6, Theorem 12, following Halmos, assumes regular invariant measures and normalizes on a compact set of finite positive Haar measure. Ordinary uniqueness for locally finite Haar measures alone cannot cover ∞·μ. The s-finite extension follows with a compactly supported nonnegative φ of μ-integral 1. For nonnegative measurable f consider ∫∫ f(x)φ(xy⁻¹)dμ(y)dν(x). Left invariance and inversion invariance of the bi-invariant μ give ∫f dν. Staton Proposition 5 permits interchanging the integrals. Substituting x=zy by right invariance of ν and integrating f(zy) over μ yields (∫φ dν)(∫f dμ), including the extended scalar conventions. Take f to be each measurable indicator. A Bourbaki statement explicitly allowing an s-finite ν and d=∞ was not located.
sources: F. van Doorn, Formalized Haar Measure, §6, Lemma 11 and Theorem 12, regular invariant measures and a compact set of positive Haar measure
S. Staton, Commutative Semantics for Probabilistic Programming, §4.2, Proposition 5, interchange for two s-finite measures and a nonnegative measurable function

exists_length_shaOdd_le.verdict: explicit finite-level estimate; main-conjecture comparison needs additional arguments
exists_length_shaOdd_le.comparison: Fix N≠0, any natural t, and a CM number field E whose specified embedding lands in the Nth cyclotomic field. The theorem produces one positive integer X at most 2^(4(N+t+3)^27) times the class number of E. For every prime ℓ, eligible coefficient ring O, exponent e<t and precision n it bounds the O-length of shaOdd(ℓ,E,O,e,n) by v_O(X). The coefficient ring is a characteristic-zero DVR finite and free over the ℓ-adic integers, with finite quotients and the stipulated roots of unity. The object is a module of locally constant cocycles. At e=0 it imposes vanishing on inertia at ℓ, with no oddness condition. For e>0 it imposes oddness under conjugation and vanishing on the kernel of the cyclotomic character in the decomposition groups at ℓ. Both cases are unramified away from ℓ. The catalogue's t≥1 hypothesis and its unrestricted description as an odd part should be corrected. Greither's Theorem 3.2 identifies an Iwasawa characteristic ideal for character components. Extracting finite-level lengths, the single simultaneous integer and its explicit archimedean size requires additional work. The pinned proof uses a Stickelberger bound, separates e=0 and controls small primes using detecting cocycles. The references give context for this quantitative statement. They do not yet supply an identified printed statement with this uniform bound.
sources: Greither, Class groups of abelian fields, and the main conjecture, Theorem 3.2, p. 469
Mazur and Wiles, Class fields of abelian extensions of Q, introduction on the Iwasawa main conjecture, pp. 179–184
Pinned definition of the local conditions and cocycle module, SelmerDefs.lean:89–97

exists_near_max.verdict: Poor–Yuen's semihull control at a Siegel maximum is an analogue. The unitary near-maximum estimate and its constant remain unlocated.
exists_near_max.comparison: For a CM-type field E, nonempty finite n and a Hermitian space V with signs s, take a nonzero rapidly decreasing form F of level ς with ς integral, ς̄=−ς and 0<Im Φ_w(ς)≤c at every archimedean place, with c≥1. Assume adelic holomorphicity for a positive-first order, gaps ≥1 between opposite signs in each weight, and |u_wi|≤B with B≥2. Some z has F(z)≠0, sup|F|≤2|F(z)|, and every g with |F(g)|≥|F(z)| has first minimum ≥1/√(Bc). This first minimum is capped at 1 and uses the moved adelic lattice. Poor–Yuen 1.2–1.3 concerns scalar Siegel modular forms on the Siegel upper half-space with translation invariance or a finite-index symplectic modular group. At an attained maximum of det(Y)^(k/2)|f| they locate k/(4π) times the inverse imaginary part in the semihull of the Fourier support, at every cusp. They do not give a unitary CM lattice estimate on an entire superlevel set. The authors' one-variable holomorphic cusp argument is related, but the group, level parameter, vector weights, near-maximum quantifier and numerical conversion to the shortest lattice vector require a new comparison.
sources: C. Poor and D. Yuen, Linear dependence among Siegel modular forms, Mathematische Annalen 318 (2000), §1, Theorems 1.2–1.3 and the discussion following them

exists_orthonormal_Ô.verdict: Orthonormalization of a unimodular integral Hermitian matrix at all finite places.
exists_orthonormal_Ô.comparison: The ring here is the integral finite adèles of a CM field containing a primitive 5040th root. The pin produces an integral z with z−z* a unit. Thus conjugation cannot act trivially on the residue field at a nonsplit prime fixed by it, excluding ramification in the quadratic extension of the real subfield. At an unramified nonsplit place Wall's classification gives a unique unimodular lattice of each rank, hence a basis with identity Gram matrix. At a split pair the Hermitian pairing is an ordinary perfect pairing of free modules on the two factors, where one chooses dual bases. The local changes of basis and their inverses assemble in the product of the local integer rings. Equality of field discriminant classes alone would not imply integral equivalence at ramified dyadic places.
sources: C. T. C. Wall, On the classification of hermitian forms I, local classification around pp. 432–433, split and unramified cases; Theorem 2 for the lift from the residue field
Jacobowitz, Hermitian forms over local fields, American Journal of Mathematics 84 (1962), 441–465, general classification

exists_prime_modEq_one_log_mem.comparison: Fix a positive multiple M of 4 and a natural A. Lean asks for one prime congruent to 1 modulo M^k, with its logarithm in [U,U+W], uniformly for the indicated k and U when W is sufficiently large. For A>0 put x=exp(U). The assumptions give q=M^k ≤ W^A ≤ (log x)^A. The estimate for primes weighted by log p gives θ(2x;q,1)−θ(x;q,1)>0 uniformly, since the totient is at most (log x)^A and the error saves more than any logarithmic power. For W≥log 2 this dyadic interval fits inside the required window. When A=0 the range of U is eventually empty. The source proves its estimate by a different analytic argument.
sources: Montgomery and Vaughan, Multiplicative Number Theory I, §11.3, Corollary 11.19, p. 381 (von Mangoldt sum), and Corollary 11.21, p. 382 (prime sum)

exists_ringEquiv_extend.verdict: Relative classification of algebraically closed fields over a countable common subring.
exists_ringEquiv_extend.comparison: The two injections make the source an integral domain and identify its fraction field inside ℂ and L. That field is countable. Each algebraically closed extension has the cardinality of the continuum, hence that transcendence degree over the common countable field. Match transcendence bases, identify the rational function fields over the base and extend to an isomorphism of their algebraic closures. The resulting isomorphism respects the two given injections. These steps justify the additional relative assertion.
sources: Stacks Project, Fields, Lemma 9.26.3, existence and cardinality of transcendence bases
Stacks Project, Fields, Lemma 9.10.6, uniqueness over the base of the algebraic closure

galRep_of_parahoric_type.verdict: The published away-from-ℓ comparison needs a local type and exponent calculation to recover these simultaneous matrix identities
galRep_of_parahoric_type.comparison: On a standard definite unitary space over a CM field with Weil data, fix a split finite place w∤ℓ and A above it. Choose a uniformizer, unit, geometric Frobenius lift s and inertia lift τ whose abelianized classes give their geometric Artin symbols, and a nonzero y in an isotypic space x. Assume y lies in the parahoric eigenspace with character c and d_i=c(diag(1,…,u,…,1)) with d_i=d_j implying the same block f(i)=f(j). For F=r_x(s), T=r_x(τ), every polynomial vanishing on the transported d_i kills T, F and T commute, and there is one torus exponent θ with an exponent functional nonzero on y such that, for all natural b, ∏_i(X−ι(θ_i(ϖ)d_i^b)) kills FT^b. Taylor–Yoshida Theorem A identifies a normalized Frobenius-semisimplified Weil–Deligne parameter of a cuspidal conjugate-self-dual GL representation square-integrable somewhere. Harris–Taylor's cited antecedent compares classes, with multiplicity in its early preprint. Neither printed statement constructs an exponent functional on y or identifies arbitrary representatives of both Artin classes in a parahoric calculation. Transfer of x to eligible GL data and the local representation calculation are substantive. The compact proof uses its eigencharacter and sorted-exponent lemmas to supply them.
sources: R. Taylor and T. Yoshida, Compatibility of local and global Langlands correspondences, Theorem A, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 20 (2007), pp. 467–468, author preprint p. 1. The local representation is Frobenius-semisimplified and carries the paper's dual and |det| twist.

M. Harris and R. Taylor, On the geometry and cohomology of some simple Shimura varieties, introduction, Theorem C, author preprint pp. 6–7. The stated comparison in the Grothendieck group has a nonzero integer multiplicity a(Π), at places away from ℓ, for a cohomological conjugate-self-dual cuspidal Π square-integrable somewhere.
T. Barnet-Lamb, T. Gee, D. Geraghty and R. Taylor, Potential automorphy and change of weight, Ann. of Math. 179 (2014), Theorem 2.1.1, p. 538, especially clauses (2)–(4).
Pinned ambient hypotheses and both complete parahoric statements.

genIndex_algebraMap.verdict: The number-field product formula evaluated on a principal finite adèle, together with the convention at zero.
genIndex_algebraMap.comparison: For x≠0 the project's index is the reciprocal of the product of the normalized finite absolute values. The product formula identifies that reciprocal with the archimedean product, |N(E/ℚ)(x)|. Complex places contribute the squared modulus. The source also allows x=0. Its zero rule for the index of a nonunit and the vanishing norm prove this case separately.
sources: Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Chapter 7, Theorem 7.15, product formula

heckeSplit_comm.verdict: Spherical Hecke commutativity for the specified double-coset operators, with an integral coefficient argument.
heckeSplit_comm.comparison: Satake proves commutativity of the bi-invariant convolution algebra for the indicated compact subgroup and treats its integer-valued subring with compact subgroup volume one. At a split unitary place the local group is GLₙ(E_w) with compact subgroup GLₙ(O_w). Its basic double-coset characteristic functions act on compact-fixed vectors by finite sums. Equality of their integer structure constants survives in the arbitrary commutative coefficient ring of the Lean representation. The two split labels can be equal, conjugate, or supported at distinct places of the fixed field. For conjugate labels the source uses the transpose/adjoint double coset in the same factor. At distinct underlying places the factors commute. Only these operators on a common fixed vector occur in the conclusion.
sources: Satake, Theory of spherical functions on reductive algebraic groups over p-adic fields, Chapter II, §5.1, Theorem 1 and the integer subring preceding it

hecke_eq_frob_on_parahoricEigenspace.verdict: A matrix-weighted identity for a specific Hecke operator requires additional parahoric linear algebra
hecke_eq_frob_on_parahoricEigenspace.comparison: Keep the same standard, split w∤ℓ, place, geometric Artin lifts and isotypic x as above. For y∈x in the parahoric eigenspace of the top-left-entry function χ, require χ(u)≠0 and χ(u)^(|n|!)≠1. For every complex polynomial G and every matrix M, with U the double-coset operator at diag(ϖ,1,…,1) on the pro-Iwahori space, the identity is ι⁻¹(tr((r(τ)−1)M))·G(U)y=ι⁻¹(tr(G^ι(r(s))(r(τ)−1)M))·y. There is no assumption trace((r(τ)−1)M)≠0 and y need not be nonzero. The local Langlands comparison of Taylor–Yoshida specifies the associated Weil–Deligne parameter. It does not act on this parahoric vector or insert an arbitrary M into an identity with the Hecke operator. The pinned proof computes the degree-one identity using a local double-coset relation and group/character decompositions, and then inducts on G. No corresponding theorem at the cited published place was located.
sources: R. Taylor and T. Yoshida, Compatibility of local and global Langlands correspondences, Theorem A, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 20 (2007), pp. 467–468, author preprint p. 1. The local representation is Frobenius-semisimplified and carries the paper's dual and |det| twist.

M. Harris and R. Taylor, On the geometry and cohomology of some simple Shimura varieties, introduction, Theorem C, author preprint pp. 6–7. The stated comparison in the Grothendieck group has a nonzero integer multiplicity a(Π), at places away from ℓ, for a cohomological conjugate-self-dual cuspidal Π square-integrable somewhere.
Pinned ambient hypotheses and both complete parahoric statements.

hecke_transfer_of_equivariant.verdict: The split local parameter correspondence is verified. The universal operator identity and its splitting-character normalization need a further comparison.
hecke_transfer_of_equivariant.comparison: Mínguez's Theorem 1 for GLₙ × GLₘ over a nonarchimedean field, n≤m and D=F, gives the contragredient parameter plus the parameter of the trivial GLₘ₋ₙ representation for the irreducible theta correspondent. This accounts for the dual input and the extra string of roots at an eigencharacter. Lean assumes a split place w, two characters unramified there, the projection-to-vacuum condition on f, m=n+k, and a linear map equivariant on the indicated translates of f. Its image is spherical for both actions. On this vector it identifies the output polynomial at w with the input polynomial at the conjugate place, evaluated at q^k A/B times X, multiplied by ∏_{j<k}(1−q^j A X). Here A and B are the respective space-character uniformizer values times q^{n/2} and q^{m/2}. Arbitrary ambient representations and possible nonsimple Hecke modules make a scalar-eigenvalue comparison insufficient. The source proves the vector identity by local residue-matrix sums.
sources: Mínguez, Correspondance de Howe explicite : paires duales de type II, introduction, Theorem 1 and the parameter formula following it, p. 718, and Corollary 6.3
Pinned definition of the uniformizer scalar including the half-power of q

highestVector_cyclic.verdict: A vanishing consequence of Schur orthogonality for a unit highest vector in a finite tensor product of compact unitary representations.
highestVector_cyclic.comparison: The place set Φ and row set n are finite. For each w the integer labels l_w need only be injective. They order the rows in the evaluation vector v for the Schur module with diagram determined by the column multiplicities κ_w of heights below |n|. The group is ∏U(n), the determinant powers e_w are arbitrary integers, and the representation uses entrywise conjugation. Its invariant Gram form gives ⟨v,v⟩=1. For u and a complex linear form f the two alternatives are ⟨v,ρ(x)u⟩=0 for every x, or f(ρ(x)v)=0 for every x. In either case Schur’s identity with a=c=v and b=u has zero integrand, while its integral equals f(u)/dim ρ. This also follows from the span of the orbit of a nonzero vector in an irreducible representation. Only the row ordering is used here. No equation equating l to a Harish-Chandra parameter is assumed.
sources: A. W. Knapp, Advanced Real Analysis, digital second edition, Chapter VI, Corollary 6.29(b), p. 249, Schur orthogonality for normalized Haar measure
Compact-group and polynomial-representation notes hosted by N. Wallach, Theorems 4.5 and 10.7, especially the Schur-character description of irreducible GL modules

hua_integral_le.verdict: The stated upper bound follows from an exact iterated beta integral with translations and a linear change in each row.
hua_integral_le.comparison: Write k for the number of columns, m for the number of integrated rows and p for the current determinant exponent. Integrating one complex row against positive definite M gives a factor π^k Γ(p−k)/(Γ(p)|det S|²) times det(M)^(1−p). Translate by the prescribed row offset, use the complex change of variables and the determinant lemma, and evaluate the resulting radial integral. The successive integer exponents run from m+r down to r+1. Since r≥k, each gamma quotient is at most 1/k!, giving the displayed power and the factor det(M)^(−r). Empty rows or columns give the direct constant case. The beta identity is located precisely. I did not locate this normalization and translated inequality as a numbered result in Hua's book.
sources: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, §5.12, equations 5.12.1 and 5.12.3
Hua, Harmonic Analysis of Functions of Several Complex Variables in the Classical Domains, bibliographic reference

ideleAbs_toAdele.verdict: The number-field product formula for the principal idèle of a totally complex field.
ideleAbs_toAdele.comparison: The norm at each complex place is the square of the ordinary absolute value, and the nonarchimedean factors have the residue-field normalization. The finite product convention omits components equal to one. With these conventions Milne's product over every place equals one for each x in E×. Lean packages those factors as the idelic module and assumes an embedding representative at each infinite place.
sources: Milne, Algebraic Number Theory, Chapter 7, Theorem 7.15

inner_product_formula.verdict: The exact shape and rank range of the classical identity are verified. The test spaces and volume normalization differ.
inner_product_formula.comparison: Li, Theorem 2.1, equation (26), expresses the inner product of two theta lifts as an integral of the product of a Weil matrix coefficient and an automorphic matrix coefficient. In Li's quadratic-extension case, ε = 1/2, hence his n > 2n′ + 4ε − 2 is precisely target rank > twice source rank. His two source vectors belong to one cuspidal representation and both Weil vectors are Schwartz–Bruhat functions. Lean allows two arbitrary rapidly decreasing automorphic functions, a free second datum f′ and a clean first datum. Clean means constant signature sign, or finite test data on conjugately disjoint places supported on matrices left-invertible at a specified place. The Lean conclusion includes integrability and the target quotient volume for its Haar measures. Comparing Li's choices of measure and extending his stated hypotheses to these spaces remain necessary. Liu's Proposition 2.3 unfolds a cuspidal Eisenstein zeta integral for Re(s)>n and decomposable data. Eischen–Harris–Li–Skinner 4.1.4 is a section on cuspidal zeta integrals.
sources: Li, Non-vanishing theorems for the cohomology of certain arithmetic quotients, case 2 on pp. 177–178 and §2, Theorem 2.1, (24)–(27), p. 184
Liu, Arithmetic theta lifting and L-derivatives for unitary groups I, §2B, Proposition 2.3, p. 862
Eischen, Harris, Li and Skinner, p-adic L-functions for unitary groups, §4.1.4, Zeta integrals

integral_eq_zero_of_lift_eq_zero.verdict: analogue in cited paper; exact published inference open
integral_eq_zero_of_lift_eq_zero.comparison: The included hypotheses specify sharp finite data for the level, a rapidly decreasing level-invariant source form, a rank inequality m>2n and vanishing of its lift. The conclusion is the vanishing of a real matrix-coefficient integral against every rapidly decreasing comparison form. The Lean proof invokes its inner-product formula, partial integrals and dual data. Rallis (1984) treats orthogonal and symplectic groups. Li gives the matching unitary stable range and a pairing of two theta lifts in Theorem 2.1. Identifying the two project test vectors, the local separation and the Haar normalizations still requires an argument.
sources: Rallis, Injectivity properties of liftings associated to Weil representations, Introduction, §1, especially Proposition 1.1 and Theorem 1.6
Li, Non-vanishing theorems for the cohomology of certain arithmetic quotients, pp. 177–178, case 2, and §2, Theorem 2.1, equation (26), p. 184

integral_quotMeasure_tsum.verdict: Unfolding for the proper left action of a countable discrete subgroup, with its counting measure and the ambient left Haar measure.
integral_quotMeasure_tsum.comparison: Let G be second-countable, locally compact and Hausdorff, Γ a discrete subgroup, μ a left Haar measure and f:G→ℂ in L¹(μ). Subgroup.qms Γ μ is βμ on G for a cutoff with Σγ β(γg)=1. The periodization Σγ f(γg) is integrable for βμ and has integral ∫f dμ. The action of the countable discrete Γ on G is proper and preserves μ. Its normalized orbital integration is the proper-action instance of Gentner–Last §2, (2.5)–(2.9), since Γ is unimodular and its orbital measure counts along Γg. Any normalized cutoff gives the same integral of an orbit-invariant function by the change of variables g↦γg and inversion of the summation index. Apply first to |f| to obtain absolute convergence βμ-almost everywhere, then apply Fubini to the real and imaginary parts. A quotient by left cosets can equivalently carry the pushforward of βμ. The unfolding holds for nonunimodular G and for Γ of infinite covolume. Right-invariance of a measure on Γ\G is a separate property.
sources: D. Gentner and G. Last, Palm pairs and the general mass-transport principle, §2, equations (2.5)–(2.9), proper Haar actions and normalized orbital measures
S. Staton, Commutative Semantics for Probabilistic Programming, §4.2, Proposition 5, interchange for two s-finite measures and a nonnegative measurable function

isCentralProj_sum_tupleIdem.verdict: Finite sums of pairwise orthogonal central idempotents for the restricted Green labels
isCentralProj_sum_tupleIdem.comparison: For the same finite family of fields and finite matrix index, s is any finite set of polynomial tuples. Each invalid tuple contributes zero. For two distinct valid tuples some local polynomials differ, hence a factor has disjoint Green character parameter. Orthogonality kills the product of the corresponding central idempotents. Their tensor products remain orthogonal and summing gives the two fields of IsCentralProj: idempotence and conjugacy-invariant coefficients. The assertion alone cannot recover irreducibility or classify characters. The empty sum and nonlabel terms are allowed. Self-adjointness is a separate consequence of the coefficient formula.
sources: J. A. Green, The characters of the finite general linear groups, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 80 (1955), §8, Theorems 13–14, pp. 441–444, especially Theorem 14 and the degree formula on pp. 443–444. The parameters assign a partition to each Frobenius orbit of multiplicative characters.
Pinned squarefree labels, character signs and the zero branch of labelIdem.
Pinned definition of IsCentralProj as two conditions on the group-algebra element and its coefficients.

isCentralProj_tupleIdem.verdict: Central idempotence for squarefree character labels, extended by zero and tensor products
isCentralProj_tupleIdem.comparison: For a finite family of finite fields k_w, a finite matrix index set n and an arbitrary tuple of polynomials c_w, the tensor of the label elements in the group algebra of ∏ GL_n(k_w) has square itself and conjugacy-invariant coefficients. Each local factor is set to zero unless c_w is monic, squarefree of degree |n|, and has nonzero constant term. For a valid label the polynomial roots determine multiplicative-character orbits via a fixed faithful character, each assigned partition (1). Green gives a distinct irreducible character for each such datum, within a classification allowing all partitions. Character orthogonality gives the local central idempotent, since its coefficient at g is Ξ(1)·conj Ξ(g)/|GL|. The tensor product preserves central idempotence. IsCentralProj does not mention an adjoint, irreducibility or primitivity. Self-adjointness in the standard finite group algebra follows separately from the character formula, even when a factor is zero.
sources: J. A. Green, The characters of the finite general linear groups, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 80 (1955), §8, Theorems 13–14, pp. 441–444, especially Theorem 14 and the degree formula on pp. 443–444. The parameters assign a partition to each Frobenius orbit of multiplicative characters.
I. G. Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., IV §6, pp. 284–286, including (6.5) and the hook-length computation (6.6).
Pinned squarefree labels, character signs and the zero branch of labelIdem.
Pinned definition of IsCentralProj as two conditions on the group-algebra element and its coefficients.

isEdge_of_isJointHarmonic.verdict: Joint compact types occur in the published real correspondence. The two-sided analytic conclusions need additional arguments.
isEdge_of_isJointHarmonic.comparison: At every infinite place the supplied polynomial is joint highest and harmonic, with matching parameters and gaps at least 500(n+n′)³ between opposite-sign entries of the half-parameters. For its product over places the output IsEdge includes, in each of two directions, a cusp kernel, a nonzero real integral of its conjugate against the oscillator coefficient, and level-conditional preservation of automorphic type. For every polynomial vector it also supplies a compactly supported convolution expressing the corresponding lift in terms of the distinguished lift. Ichino Lemma 7.8 gives a necessary and sufficient highest-weight criterion for two local compact types to correspond in joint harmonics, with specified splitting characters. Ichino Proposition 7.2 equates existence of some nonzero local coefficient integral with nonzero theta lift in its rank range. Howe's Theorem 1 identifies irreducible oscillator quotients. The specific integral for every admissible polynomial and the global convolution identities require further argument. Nonvanishing here concerns that real integral.
sources: Ichino, Theta lifting for discrete series representations of real unitary groups, §7.2, Proposition 7.2, and §7.4, Lemma 7.8 and the convention discussion in its proof, pp. 35–36 of the preprint
Howe, Transcending classical invariant theory, Theorem 1 and Theorem 1A
Pinned definitions of IsHalfEdge and IsEdge

isFiniteTypeAt_char.verdict: The weight-zero potentially unramified case of Conrad's local character calculation, with its scalar Weil polynomial.
isFiniteTypeAt_char.comparison: Take an embedded number field E, a closure place A, and a continuous character μ:Gal(Ω/E)→Q̄_ℓˣ with finite inertia image at A. The matrix index has one element. Above ℓ the conclusion is potential crystallinity, the single jump 0 at each compatible embedding, and annihilation of the linear Weil operator by X−μ(s) at every compatible Weil pair. Away from ℓ, LocalEmbedding.lean:35–52 reduces finite type to near-identity inertia acting trivially and the polynomial to scalar matrix evaluation. Locally above ℓ, local reciprocity splits μ as a finite-order character on units extended trivially on a uniformizer and an unramified character. Their values lie in a finite coefficient field generated by the inertia values and one Frobenius value. Conrad B.3 computes the weights of the unramified factor from its zero algebraic exponents. B.4(i) makes it crystalline and B.4(ii) computes its Frobenius as the inverse of its value at arithmetic Artin of the uniformizer. Thus the eigenvalue at geometric Frobenius is its character value in the compact convention. The finite factor becomes trivial over a finite extension. On its potentially crystalline period line the Weil action is its original scalar character. Multiplying the two gives μ(s) for all the stated Weil pairs. Finite inertia allows potential crystallinity even when the original finite-order factor ramifies.
sources: B. Conrad, Lifting global representations with local properties, Appendix B, Definition B.1 and Propositions B.3 and B.4(i)–(ii), pp. 32–36
J.-M. Fontaine, Représentations ℓ-adiques potentiellement semi-stables, Exposé VIII, §2.3.7, Weil action and Frobenius convention

isIdempotentKernel_psiInFrame.verdict: Formal-degree orthogonality accounts for the integral identity. The explicit integrability threshold and normalization require separate work.
isIdempotentKernel_psiInFrame.comparison: In positive rank the authors transport a particular matrix coefficient through a Hermitian sign frame and multiply it by their formal degree. The conclusion includes continuity, absolute integrability, the inversion law, a nonzero value at the identity and a rank-one identity for every pair of translates. Harish-Chandra's square-integrable orthogonality gives the formal-degree factor after choosing Haar measure. Square integrability alone does not give absolute integrability. I found no place in the cited paper identifying this coefficient and compact-dual Haar measure with the explicit large-gap condition of the pinned code. The Lean proof uses a prior large-gap theorem and proves the frame transport.
sources: Harish-Chandra, Discrete series for semisimple Lie groups II, pp. 87–88, definition and square-integrable orthogonality

isUnitaryRep_detTwist.verdict: Strongly continuous Hilbert unitarity is verified. The degree bound is for a different operator norm.
isUnitaryRep_detTwist.comparison: Davidson Theorem 1.12 proves that the explicitly normalized oscillator action is a continuous unitary representation on the Hilbert Fock space. Pullback along a continuous group homomorphism and twisting by the unit-modulus character det(g)^γ preserve that Hilbert assertion. Lean works on the L¹ space of vacuum coefficients, equips it with the positive hermitian form realInner, and assumes a bound ‖f(g)‖ ≤ a‖g‖ on the matrix homomorphism. It asserts continuity there, preservation and positivity of the form, and a bound of order ‖g‖^{|C|} on the Banach operator norm, where C indexes the target sign matrix. Lean derives the last bound from the integrated-action estimate and the specific multiplier. Theorem 1.12 supplies no estimate in that Banach norm.
sources: Davidson, The harmonic representation of U(p,q), formulas (1.9a–b) and Theorem 1.12, pp. 39–40

labelChar_degree_bounds.verdict: A quantitative lower bound obtained from Green's exact degree
labelChar_degree_bounds.comparison: Let k have q elements, K be an algebraically closed extension with an injective multiplicative character T into ℂ, and c a monic squarefree polynomial of degree r=|n| with c(0)≠0. For d=Ξ_c(1), Lean gives Re d≥0 and d·conj(d)/|GL_r(k)|≥(1−r/q)q^(−r). Match distinct Frobenius orbits of degrees e_j with partition (1). Green's exact positive degree is ∏_{i=1}^r(q^i−1)/∏_j(q^{e_j}−1). Since Σe_j=r, the denominator is at most q^r. Substituting the order of GL_r gives d²/|GL|≥q^(−r)∏_{i=1}^r(1−q^(−i))≥q^(−r)(1−r/q). This covers r=0 and imposes no q>r assumption. The Lean declaration asks for positivity and an inequality only.
sources: J. A. Green, The characters of the finite general linear groups, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 80 (1955), §8, Theorems 13–14, pp. 441–444, especially Theorem 14 and the degree formula on pp. 443–444. The parameters assign a partition to each Frobenius orbit of multiplicative characters.
I. G. Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., IV §6, pp. 284–286, including (6.5) and the hook-length computation (6.6).
Pinned squarefree labels, character signs and the zero branch of labelIdem.

letterPoly_highestVector_holomorphic.verdict: The one-sign highest polynomial specializes the published minor construction. The full analytic conclusion needs the normed-model comparison.
letterPoly_highestVector_holomorphic.comparison: Fix a sign c, an injective parameter determining an order within each sign, a positive-first order O, and a column multiplicity function at each infinite place. The length bound selects one family of minors in the c variables. This is the one-block instance of the initial/terminal minor products in Davidson Theorem 2.9. Lean applies the staircase construction place by place and obtains a nonzero polynomial. It also proves that its coefficients under every continuous functional have triangular analytic extensions for the determinant-twisted, place-dependent staircase weight. Davidson gives the highest weights in local coordinates and a Hilbert holomorphic realization in Theorem 3.6. The change to the project's Banach coefficient tests and its weight conventions has not been deduced from those theorems.
sources: Davidson, The harmonic representation of U(p,q), Theorem 2.9, p. 45, and Theorem 3.6, p. 48
Kashiwara and Vergne, On the Segal–Shale–Weil representations and harmonic polynomials, Chapter III, Proposition 6.1 and (6.2), p. 44

linearFrob_apply.verdict: Fontaine gives the signed Weil action on classical periods. The stated B_max-linear extension on arbitrary modules remains unlocated.
linearFrob_apply.comparison: With Γ over G_p of open image, R any commutative Z_p-algebra and T an R-module with compatible Z_p action, assume near-identity fixed periods span B_max⊗T. Take m≥0 and s in Γ with j(s)⁻¹ acting on residues as the p^m-power map. For each d fixed near 1 the chosen B_max-linear β_{s,m} agrees on d with (φ^m j(s))⊗ρ(s). The definition at Crystalline/Defs.lean:103–107 uses choice, so existence of this linear extension is mathematical content. Fontaine VIII §2.3.7 defines the period-ring action of w by φ^(−a(w))w, then combines it with the action on V. Geometric Frobenius explains the sign in the compact formula. Fontaine works on the potentially semistable period module of a finite-dimensional continuous representation. A source extending his operator to B_max⊗T under the stated open-image and spanning assumptions is missing.
sources: J.-M. Fontaine, Représentations ℓ-adiques potentiellement semi-stables, Astérisque 223, Exposé VIII (1994), §§2.3.2–2.3.3 and §2.3.7, especially pp. 339–340

lintegral_orbitMeasure_lintegral.verdict: The integral equality holds for arbitrary measurable actions with an inversion-invariant s-finite group measure and a cutoff. This exceeds the cited proper Haar-action setting.
lintegral_orbitMeasure_lintegral.comparison: For nonnegative measurable f:X→[0,∞], a jointly measurable H-action, s-finite invariant μ on X and s-finite inversion-invariant ν on H, the chosen β satisfies ∫β(hx)dν(h)=1 pointwise. The outer integral is on X with measure βμ, and ∫_X∫_H f(hx)dν(h)β(x)dμ(x)=∫_X f dμ, with infinite integrals allowed. In Gentner–Last §2, (2.9), the orbit measures are translates of Haar and the group is locally compact second-countable, the operation proper, and the invariant measure σ-finite. Their attribution to Kallenberg does not identify a theorem for arbitrary ν or arbitrary measurable X. The full claimed equality follows directly by applying Staton’s Proposition 5 to β(x)f(hx), using μ-invariance to obtain f(y)β(h⁻¹y) and ν-invariance under inversion to evaluate the orbit integral at 1. This also follows by integrating against the pinned action-map pushforward.
sources: D. Gentner and G. Last, Palm pairs and the general mass-transport principle, §2, equations (2.5)–(2.9), proper Haar actions and normalized orbital measures

O. Kallenberg, Invariant measures and disintegrations with applications to Palm and related kernels, Probability Theory and Related Fields 139 (2007), 285–310. Publisher abstract. The numbered identities are given explicitly by Gentner–Last §2
S. Staton, Commutative Semantics for Probabilistic Programming, §4.2, Proposition 5, interchange for two s-finite measures and a nonnegative measurable function

matrix_gauss_sum.verdict: The finite-field identity for invertible frequencies is located. The full finite-ring statement has a different scope.
matrix_gauss_sum.comparison: Kondo sums an irreducible GLₙ(F_q)-representation against the trace character. At invertible A his p. 244 change of variables gives the inverse representation factor, and his main theorem evaluates the remaining scalar. With the determinant character and its extension by zero this explains the invertible-frequency law over a field. Lean works over every finite commutative ring with a primitive additive character and a multiplicative character nontrivial on suitable units of the form 1+ca for each nonzero a. Its input S is any determinant-equivariant function on all matrices. It proves a formula at every frequency, including singular ones, and a product identity with the conjugate determinant Gauss sum by Fourier inversion. Kondo discusses singular frequencies for certain characters in §2.3. The passage to arbitrary finite rings and this general S is unverified from that article.
sources: Kondo, On Gaussian sums attached to the general linear groups over finite fields, pp. 244–245, and §2.3, pp. 253–254

measurePreserving_orbitMeasure.verdict: The claimed Kallenberg specialization has incompatible measure hypotheses. The exact pushforward follows from s-finite Tonelli and the two invariances.
measurePreserving_orbitMeasure.comparison: A group H with measurable inversion acts jointly measurably on X. The measure μ on X is s-finite and H-invariant. The s-finite measure ν on H is inversion-invariant and need not be Haar. A measurable β:X→[0,∞] with ∫β(hx)dν(h)=1 for every x is given by HasCutoff. The chosen orbitMeasure ν μ is βμ on X. The action map (x,h)↦hx sends (βμ)×ν to μ. Gentner–Last §2, (2.5) and (2.9), records Kallenberg Lemma 2.1 and Theorem 2.4 for a proper action of a locally compact second-countable group on a standard Borel space, with Haar orbital measures and a σ-finite invariant measure. These hypotheses need not hold in Lean. Staton, Proposition 5, permits interchanging the two integrals of β(x)f(hx) for each nonnegative indicator f. Change x to h⁻¹y using μ-invariance and invert h using ν-invariance. The inner integral ∫β(h⁻¹y)dν(h) is 1. Equality for every measurable set gives exactly the pushforward. The exact formulation as a named instance of Kallenberg’s theorem remains open.
sources: D. Gentner and G. Last, Palm pairs and the general mass-transport principle, §2, equations (2.5)–(2.9), proper Haar actions and normalized orbital measures

O. Kallenberg, Invariant measures and disintegrations with applications to Palm and related kernels, Probability Theory and Related Fields 139 (2007), 285–310. Publisher abstract. The numbered identities are given explicitly by Gentner–Last §2
S. Staton, Commutative Semantics for Probabilistic Programming, §4.2, Proposition 5, interchange for two s-finite measures and a nonnegative measurable function

minkowski_second.verdict: Bombieri–Vaaler Theorem 3 gives the claimed constant after passing from their product body to a joint Euclidean norm and rounding the radii to powers of two.
minkowski_second.comparison: Take E CM with f complex places, d=2f, rank n, rd=|disc E|^{1/d} and y∈GL_n(𝔸_E). The vectors form an E-basis. For each column Y_j, y⁻¹Y_j must be finite-integral and have joint Euclidean norm over all infinite places at most 2^{x_j}, with arbitrary integer exponents x_j. In Bombieri–Vaaler’s (3.1) take the finite modules y_v𝒪_vⁿ and, at each complex embedding, the image under y_v of the Euclidean ball of radius 1/√f in ℂⁿ. Each product-body radius r bounds the joint norm by r. In their covolume-one normalization the volume of this body is |det y|_𝔸 · 2^{fn}|disc E|^{−n/2} · (πⁿ/n!)^f f^{−fn}. The factor 2^{fn}|disc E|^{−n/2} comes from the ordinary real covolume (2^{−f}√|disc E|)^n of 𝒪_Eⁿ. Theorem 3 gives (∏r_j)^d vol≤2^{dn} for the E-successive minima. By discreteness the corresponding bounds are attained in the closed bodies. Choose independent vectors successively and set x_j=ceil(log₂ r_j). Dyadic rounding costs at most 2^{dn} after raising the product to d. The resulting bound on |det y|_𝔸·2^{dΣx_j} is 8^{fn}|disc E|^{n/2}(n!)^f f^{fn}/π^{fn}≤(8fn·rd)^{fn}. For rank zero the empty basis has determinant one. A separate verification uses Henk’s real Theorem 1.3 on the joint Euclidean ball. Since an E-subspace of rank j−1 has real Minkowski dimension d(j−1), the (d(j−1)+1)-st real successive minimum supplies the next E-independent vector. Multiplying these block bounds gives the same claimed constant with (fn)!/π^{fn} in the unsimplified joint-ball estimate.
sources: E. Bombieri and J. Vaaler, On Siegel’s lemma, §§II.2–III.1, Theorem 3, equation (3.3), pp. 16–18, adelic successive minima
M. Henk, Successive minima and lattice points, Theorem 1.3 and its proof in §3, upper bound in Minkowski’s second theorem for general real lattices

norm_sub_le_of_holomorphic_bdd.verdict: A centre-to-point bound derived by restricting to a complex line and applying the scalar Schwarz lemma.
norm_sub_le_of_holomorphic_bdd.comparison: Both E and F are complex normed spaces. The variables are redeclared at lines 75–76 without a finite-dimensional assumption. On the ball of radius r the function is complex differentiable and has norm at most B. Restrict to the line through c and z, subtract f(c) and apply a norm-one linear functional on F that norms this difference. The scalar function vanishes at the centre and has modulus at most 2B, so Schwarz's lemma gives (2B/r)‖z−c‖. When B=0 the result is immediate. The statement does not give the derivative estimate or the equality case of Schwarz's lemma.
sources: Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, §12.2, Schwarz's lemma

ostrowski_taussky.verdict: Equivalent to the determinant inequality for a matrix with positive Hermitian part, including its semidefinite endpoint.
ostrowski_taussky.comparison: Set R=(Θ+Θ*)/2. Lean permits any positive semidefinite H≤2R and gives |det H|≤2^n |det Θ|. If H is singular the inequality is immediate. Otherwise R is positive definite, determinant monotonicity gives det H≤2^n det R, and Ostrowski–Taussky gives det R≤|det Θ|. Conversely H=2R recovers the usual inequality for R>0. This equivalence concerns the inequality only. The declaration includes no equality criterion.
sources: Ostrowski and Taussky, On the variation of the determinant of a positive definite matrix, Indagationes Mathematicae 13 (1951), 383–385. The inequality is identified and restated in the introduction on p. 331 of this paper

period_eq_zero.verdict: Walls's stabilizer-period identity is for a different dual pair; the project proves the unitary vanishing separately
period_eq_zero.comparison: Let E have a CM type and Weil data, n ≃ n₁⊕n₂ finite with the specified compatible signature identification, and let Y be continuous on the standard definite unitary group, invariant on the left by rational points, with the stated K_f level above T and its conjugate. Assume the project's DescentsVanish for the split hyperbolic unitary space of rank n₁, the specified splitting character υ^|n₁|, T and Y. For every first-block h₁ the integral of Y(block(h₁,u)) over the adelic quotient of the complementary definite unitary group vanishes. Walls Prop 2.1.1 unfolds a nondegenerate Fourier coefficient for a symplectic–orthogonal pair, with matching Schwartz data, into a stabilizer period of a convolved cusp form. Rallis treats orthogonal–symplectic towers. Neither place proves this unitary statement or passes directly from orthogonality to the chosen theta kernels to pointwise vanishing of each period. The compact source identifies the unitary stabilizer of an inclusion matrix, uses compactness/continuity in the definite case, and unfolds and separates test functions to deduce the conclusion.
sources: P. Walls, The theta correspondence, periods of automorphic forms and special values of standard automorphic L-functions, §§1.1–1.2 and §2.1, Proposition 2.1.1, equation (2.1.5), pp. 5–6. The group pair is symplectic–orthogonal and the right side is the stabilizer period of a convolved cusp form.
S. Rallis, On the Howe duality conjecture, Compositio Math. 51 (1984), introduction pp. 333–335. The formulation concerns the symplectic–orthogonal theta correspondence and its towers.
Unitary setup and explicit stabilizer in the compact proof.

pow_torsionOrder_eq_one.verdict: Kronecker's first theorem for integral norm-one elements of a CM field, with the torsion-group exponent supplied
pow_torsionOrder_eq_one.comparison: Let E be any CM number field and γ a norm-one element, integral over ℤ. Each complex embedding carries CM conjugation to complex conjugation, so every conjugate of γ has modulus one. Kronecker's original first theorem phrases the condition with all the roots nonreal. A real conjugate here is ±1, in which case irreducibility over ℚ already gives γ=±1. In the remaining case apply his theorem to the monic minimal polynomial. The order of the resulting root of unity divides torsionOrder E, the cardinality of the finite group of torsion units of E, by Lagrange's theorem. No primitive generator of that group is needed.
sources: L. Kronecker, Zwei Sätze über Gleichungen mit ganzzahligen Coefficienten, J. reine angew. Math. 53 (1857), pp. 173–175, Satz I beginning on p. 173. The digitized Werke I reprint gives the theorem on p. 105.

prod_mem_holomorphicData.verdict: Local holomorphic highest-weight realization is located. The coefficient test on the project's normed model remains a separate assertion.
prod_mem_holomorphicData.comparison: Given a positive-first order, the prescribed ordering within each sign and one joint highest polynomial at every infinite place, Lean forms their product in disjoint variables. It proves nonvanishing and tests holomorphy against every bounded linear functional on its Fock space. Each scalar coefficient extends analytically at the specified unitary-times-triangular matrices with the given triangular weight. Kashiwara–Vergne III, Theorems 6.3 and 7.2, describe the compact weights and highest-weight constituents for a single real U(p,q). Davidson §3.3 and Theorem 3.6 realize such a constituent on a Hilbert space of vector-valued holomorphic functions on the matrix disk. The stronger topology of the project's L¹ coefficient model changes its continuous dual. The identification of every such functional, the triangular covariance and the finite product are the extra steps in this formulation.
sources: Kashiwara and Vergne, On the Segal–Shale–Weil representations and harmonic polynomials, Chapter III, Theorems 6.3 and 7.2, pp. 44–45
Davidson, The harmonic representation of U(p,q), §3.3 and Theorems 3.5–3.6, pp. 47–48

q_binomial_submodule.verdict: The finite q-binomial theorem in its subspace-counting form.
q_binomial_submodule.comparison: Group the summands indexed by subspaces of W by dimension j. The number in dimension j is the Gaussian binomial coefficient, and the weight is (−X)^j q^(j(j−1)/2). Substituting −X in Stanley's identity yields the product over 0≤a<dim W of (1−q^a X). The text and the Lean expression agree for finite fields, including W=0 with both sides equal to one.
sources: Stanley, Enumerative Combinatorics, vol. 1, second edition, Proposition 1.7.2 and equation (1.87), including the finite-field proof

rallis_inner_product_euler.verdict: analogue in cited paper; claimed special case unsupported by that citation
rallis_inner_product_euler.comparison: Lean produces a single nonzero constant A for the fixed real edge. For each permitted choice of characters and sharp finite data it gives injectivity on forms of level J and a convergent explicit coset sum for the Petersson pairing of two lifts. Rallis §1 studies a different dual pair. Li §2 supplies the unitary pairing in the right rank range for cusp-representation vectors and Schwartz data. The nonzero constant uniform in the allowed data, the project measures, the evaluation as the stated coset sum and the deduction of injectivity are further assertions.
sources: Rallis, Injectivity properties of liftings associated to Weil representations, §1 and Theorem 1.6
Li, Non-vanishing theorems for the cohomology of certain arithmetic quotients, §2, Theorem 2.1, equation (26), p. 184

realAction.verdict: Explicit multiplier and proof of composition. The exact kernel normalization remains to be identified.
realAction.comparison: realAction directly supplies the matrix action and the scalar realMultiplier(g), the complex conjugate of the determinant of the negative–negative block. Its fields establish preservation of the Heisenberg pairing and measure, continuity and the Gaussian composition identity. Lines 32–51 prove the last field with a complex Gaussian integral. There is no choice of an unspecified splitting in this definition. Davidson §1 explicitly fixes phases for the Fock intertwiners, and Theorem 1.12 proves they yield a continuous genuine representation of U(p,q). Formula (1.9a) uses Davidson's polarization and kernel scalar. A conversion of that scalar into this negative-block multiplier, accounting for the vacuum and the placement of inverses, has not been verified.
sources: Davidson, The harmonic representation of U(p,q) and its connection with the generalized unit disk, §1, formula (1.9a), Lemma 1.11 and Theorem 1.12, pp. 39–40

reproducing_formula_modKernel.verdict: The classical Siegel basis theorem and the unitary stable-range pairing are located. The finite unitary reproducing formula is distinct.
reproducing_formula_modKernel.comparison: Böcherer's Theorem III spans the space of degree-n Siegel modular forms of scalar weight k by theta series for k divisible by four and k>2n. Li's Theorem 2.1 gives a stable-range pairing for theta lifts of cusp-representation vectors. Lean fixes two unitary groups, the second definite of rank n′>2n, a nonzero principal ideal level with nonempty support, character weights, and a nonzero holomorphic Fock vector with integrable dominant-weight coefficient. At each definite class the specified finite list of polynomials must span its real compact-group translates. For each evaluation point x there are coefficients, independent of the rapid level-N function, expressing its convolution at x as a finite sum of pairings with explicit theta kernels. The proof uses the sharp datum attached to the inclusion matrix, realConv_eq_zero_of_lift_eq_zero, and a finite linear-duality argument. Neither published statement supplies these class-by-class finite test vectors or the point-evaluation identity.
sources: Böcherer, Über die Fourier-Jacobi-Entwicklung Siegelscher Eisensteinreihen, §1, Theorem III, p. 22
Li, Non-vanishing theorems for the cohomology of certain arithmetic quotients, §2, Theorem 2.1, p. 184

scalar_of_commute_schur.verdict: The scalar-commutant conclusion is Schur's lemma once irreducibility of the specified action has been proved.
scalar_of_commute_schur.comparison: Over ℂ an endomorphism commuting with an irreducible finite-dimensional representation is scalar. Lean imposes commutation with every tuple of unitary matrices acting by its concrete Schur matrices. Passage from the abstract assertion to this basis requires identifying the representation and proving irreducibility for the product. The pinned proof uses Zariski density of the unitary subgroup and a cyclic polynomial vector. Schur's lemma alone does not identify the basis of minors selected elsewhere in the project.
sources: Goodman and Wallach, Symmetry, Representations, and Invariants, §4.1.2, Lemma 4.1.4 and Corollary 4.1.5
Akin, Buchsbaum and Weyman, Schur functors and Schur complexes, Theorem II.2.16, p. 232, the standard-tableau basis

seesaw_periods.verdict: application of a located classical identity with additional hypotheses
